title: Food webs: what happens when one link disappears

summary.text: Hunters once killed almost all the sea otters around many islands of the North Pacific. Soon the tall seaweed forests there were gone too, though nobody had cut any seaweed. Sea otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins eat seaweed. A food web joins all the living beings of a place by who eats whom. So a change to one being passes on to others. Your child counts the links in a web and tests which kind of web loses more when beings disappear. They also find out what keeps numbers in nature steady.
summary.art: A split picture of the sea floor: on the left a sea otter floating above a tall kelp forest, on the right bare rock covered with spiny sea urchins and no otter.

intro.hook: A farmer finds a rat snake in her paddy field. Her neighbours tell her to kill him. The snake has never eaten one grain of paddy. Would her harvest be bigger or smaller without him?
intro.text: A rat snake eats rats, and rats eat paddy. So the snake and the paddy are joined, though the snake never touches a grain. A food web is a map of all such links in one place. In this unit you learn to read that map. You find out what happens to a web when one being disappears, and why some webs cope better than others. You also find out what keeps the numbers of plants and animals steady from year to year.
intro.art: A woman farmer at the edge of a green paddy field looking at a long rat snake sliding along the bund, with a rat peeping from a hole nearby.

outcomes: By the end I can draw a food web for a real place, count the links and say what the arrows mean.
By the end I can sort animals into herbivores, carnivores, omnivores and scavengers, and say what decomposers do.
By the end I can follow a change through a web step by step, and tell a direct effect from an indirect effect.
By the end I can explain, with my Two Webs Test results, why eaters with many foods cope better with a loss.
By the end I can explain natural balance as births and deaths that match, using the Leaky Bottle.
By the end I can explain why prey animals have many young, and why the numbers of eaters follow their food late.
By the end I can give real examples of what happened when people removed or added a being, and say what scientists still argue about.

terms.meaning: A map of who eats whom in one place. It is made of many food chains that cross, because most animals eat more than one food.
terms.example: In a forest web, a leopard eats chital, hares, langurs and peafowl. Four chains meet at the leopard.
terms.art: A hand-drawn web of ten forest beings joined by arrows, with four arrows ending at a leopard.

terms.meaning: One arrow in a food web. It joins one food to one eater, and points from the food to the eater.
terms.example: Grass → hare is one link. It shows that food passes from the grass to the hare.
terms.art: A single thick arrow from a clump of grass to a hare, labelled 'one link'.

terms.meaning: A living being who makes their own food from sunlight, air and water. Green plants and algae are producers. Every food web starts with them.
terms.example: Paddy, grass, a fig tree and the green algae in a pond are all producers.
terms.art: A paddy plant, a fig tree and green pond algae under a bright sun.

terms.meaning: A living being who cannot make their own food and must eat other living beings. All animals are consumers, including humans.
terms.example: A grasshopper, a frog, a rat snake and a child eating idli are all consumers.
terms.art: A grasshopper on a leaf, a frog, a snake and a child with a plate of idli, in a row.

terms.meaning: An animal who eats only plants.
terms.example: A chital deer, an elephant, a hare and a grasshopper are herbivores.
terms.art: A chital deer and an elephant feeding on leaves and grass.

terms.meaning: An animal who eats only other animals.
terms.example: A leopard, a frog, a spider and a rat snake are carnivores. A frog counts, because insects are animals.
terms.art: A frog catching a fly with her tongue, beside a leopard.

terms.meaning: An animal who eats both plants and animals.
terms.example: A crow, a bear, a peafowl and a human are omnivores.
terms.art: A crow with a piece of fruit and a beetle, beside a child eating rice and fish.

terms.meaning: An animal who eats animals that are already dead.
terms.example: A vulture feeds on dead cattle. A crow or a jackal will scavenge too, though they also hunt.
terms.art: Two vultures on the ground beside a dead buffalo, with a crow waiting nearby.

terms.meaning: A living being who breaks dead plants and animals down into simple matter that goes back to the soil. Most decomposers are fungi and bacteria.
terms.example: The white mould on an old chapati and the mushrooms on a wet log are decomposers at work.
terms.art: A fallen log on a forest floor with mushrooms and white threads of fungus growing on the wood.

terms.meaning: A predator is an animal who hunts and eats other animals. The animals they hunt are their prey.
terms.example: An owl is a predator and a rat is her prey. A frog is a predator of flies and the prey of snakes.
terms.art: A barn owl flying low over a field at night with a rat running below.

terms.meaning: All the living beings of one kind in one place.
terms.example: All the chital in Mudumalai forest are one population. All the rats in one village are another.
terms.art: A herd of about thirty chital deer in a forest clearing.

terms.meaning: A specialist eats one food, or very few. A generalist eats many kinds of food.
terms.example: A koala eats almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves, so koalas are specialists. A crow eats nearly anything, so crows are generalists.
terms.art: A koala holding a eucalyptus branch on one side, and a crow among fruit, grain and scraps on the other.

terms.meaning: A direct effect passes along one link, from an eater to their food or from a food to their eater. An indirect effect passes through a third being in between.
terms.example: A rat snake eats rats. That is a direct effect on the rats. Fewer rats means more paddy. That is the snake's indirect effect on the paddy.
terms.art: Three pictures in a row, paddy, rat and rat snake, with a curved dotted arrow from the snake over the rat to the paddy.

terms.meaning: A change at the top of a food chain that passes down, step by step, to the plants. 'Trophic' means 'to do with feeding'.
terms.example: Fewer sea otters led to more sea urchins, and more sea urchins led to less seaweed.
terms.art: A stair of three steps going down: an otter crossed out, many urchins, then a few stumps of seaweed.

terms.meaning: A kind of living being whose loss changes the whole web far more than their small numbers would suggest. A species is one kind of living being.
terms.example: On one rocky shore, taking away one kind of starfish cut the kinds of animals from 15 to 8.
terms.art: A purple starfish on a rock among mussels, barnacles and limpets.

terms.meaning: The way numbers in nature stay within a range from year to year. It happens when births and deaths roughly match.
terms.example: A forest may hold about the same number of chital for many years. Yet chital are born and die every day.
terms.art: A see-saw with a fawn on one side and a leopard on the other, held level.

terms.meaning: When a change causes something that pushes back against that change. Feedback is what brings a number back towards its usual level.
terms.example: When there are more deer, each deer finds less food and predators find them more easily. So more deer die, and the number comes down again.
terms.art: A loop of arrows: more deer, less food each, more deaths, fewer deer.

terms.meaning: A kind of living being whom people bring to a new place. There they spread so fast that others are harmed.
terms.example: Lantana, a garden shrub brought to India about 200 years ago, now covers the ground in many forests.
terms.art: A forest floor covered in a thicket of lantana with small pink and yellow flowers, and a chital standing beside the bushes.

terms.meaning: A simple copy of a real thing. We make one to test ideas that are too big or too slow to test for real. A model always leaves some things out.
terms.example: In the Two Webs Test, cards and arrows on paper stand for a whole forest.
terms.art: A sheet of paper with a drawn food web and coins placed on the names, beside a small picture of a real forest.

explanations.concept: From chains to webs: counting the links
explanations.definition: A food chain is one line of who eats whom, starting with a producer. A food web is all the chains of one place drawn together. Each arrow is one link, and points from the food to the eater.
explanations.description: A chain such as grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle has 5 beings and 4 links. But a frog also eats flies, and a snake also eats rats. When you add what each animal really eats, the chain becomes a web with many more links. Scientists measure a web by counting. They count the beings, count the links, and divide to find the links for each being. A web with more links for each being has more paths for food to travel along. Every path still starts at a producer, because only producers make food from sunlight.
examples: In Chain to Web, a chain with 4 links grew into a web with about 12 links.
In the Two Webs Test, the narrow web has 10 beings and 7 links. The wide web has the same 10 beings and 18 links.
A real web is far bigger. Scientists who mapped one small pond in England found nearly 200 links among 25 kinds of animal.
explanations.art: On the left a straight chain of five beings with four arrows. On the right the same five beings with extra beings and many crossing arrows.

explanations.definition: Herbivores eat plants. Carnivores eat other animals. Omnivores eat both. Scavengers eat animals that are already dead. Decomposers, mostly fungi and bacteria, break down whatever is left and return it to the soil.
explanations.description: These five words describe what a being eats, and many beings fit more than one. A jackal hunts and also scavenges. A bear eats fruit, honey, termites and fish. A crow does almost everything. So the groups are useful, but real animals do not always fit one group. Decomposers finish every chain. They break dead leaves, droppings and bodies into simple matter. Plants take that matter up through their roots and build new leaves with it. So matter goes round the web again and again, while each meal's energy is used and leaves as heat.
examples: Herbivores include the horse, the buffalo, the elephant and the chital. Carnivores include the tiger, the leopard, the frog and the cat.
Omnivores include humans, crows, bears and peafowl. A dog eats many foods too.
Scavengers include vultures and hyenas. A kite and a jackal scavenge and also hunt.
Decomposers include the mould on old bread, mushrooms, and soil bacteria too small to see.
explanations.art: Five panels: a buffalo grazing, a frog with a fly, a crow with fruit and a beetle, a vulture at a carcass, and mushrooms on a dead log.

explanations.concept: When a link is lost, the change travels both ways
explanations.definition: A change to one being in a web passes to others along the links. It travels up, to those who eat that being. It also travels down, to those whom that being eats.
explanations.description: Two rules help you follow a change. Rule one: when a food becomes scarce, their eaters go hungry and become fewer. Rule two: when an eater becomes scarce, their food is eaten less and becomes more plentiful. A change that passes along one link is a direct effect. A change that passes on through a third being is an indirect effect. If people kill the rat snakes in a field, the rats increase. That is direct. Then the paddy decreases, though no snake ever ate paddy. That is indirect. In a web, two paths can push the same being in opposite ways. Then nobody can tell the result without counting in a real field.
examples: In Take the Snakes Away, removing the snakes pushed the paddy down through the rats. It also pushed the paddy up, through the frogs and grasshoppers.
India stopped the export of frogs' legs in 1987. One reason was that frogs eat insects who damage crops.
Insect poison sprayed on paddy also kills spiders. In many Asian countries, plant-sucking insects called brown planthoppers then multiplied, because their hunters were gone.
explanations.art: A small field web of paddy, rat, grasshopper, frog, rat snake and owl. The snake is crossed out, with up arrows beside rat and frog and a down arrow beside grasshopper.

explanations.definition: A trophic cascade is a change at the top of a food chain that passes down to the plants. A keystone species is one whose loss changes the whole web far more than their numbers would suggest.
explanations.description: Sea otters were hunted for their fur until very few were left. In 1974, James Estes and John Palmisano compared islands in Alaska. Around the islands with otters, tall seaweed called kelp grew thick, and fish lived among the kelp. Around the islands without otters, big sea urchins covered the rock and had eaten the kelp down. The change had passed down three steps, from otter to urchin to kelp. A keystone species does not have to be a predator. Fig trees fruit when few other trees do, so many birds and monkeys depend on them. Elephants open paths and spread seeds. What marks a keystone is how much changes when they go.
examples: Robert Paine removed one kind of starfish from a rocky shore. Mussels took over, and the kinds of animals there fell from 15 to 8.
When most of India's vultures died, stray dogs are thought to have grown in number.
A fig tree in fruit in a dry month feeds barbets, mynas, hornbills, langurs and bats.
explanations.art: Two sea-floor scenes: one with a sea otter eating an urchin above thick kelp and fish, the other with no otter, bare rock and hundreds of urchins.

explanations.concept: Specialists and generalists: why a wide web loses fewer
explanations.definition: A specialist depends on one food. A generalist can switch to another food when one is lost. A web in which eaters have many foods loses fewer beings when some disappear.
explanations.description: In the Two Webs Test, you took the same three beings out of two paper webs. In the narrow web, each eater had only one food. When that food went, the eater starved, and then whoever ate that eater starved too. In the wide web, most eaters had two, three or four foods, so most of them lived. In 2002, Jennifer Dunne and her team did the same test on a computer with 16 real food webs. Webs with more links lost fewer extra beings. The model leaves something out. It follows hunger only. It does not show what happens when a predator is lost and their prey multiply.
examples: In the narrow web, losing the grass alone also starves the grasshopper, the hare, the peafowl and the dhole. Five beings are lost.
In the wide web, losing any one being starves nobody else.
The giant panda eats almost only bamboo. When bamboo flowers and dies over a whole hillside, pandas there have gone hungry.
explanations.art: Two paper food webs side by side with the same ten beings: one with few arrows and many beings crossed out, one with many arrows and few crossed out.

explanations.concept: Natural balance: births and deaths that match
explanations.definition: A population stays about the same size when births and deaths roughly match. Natural balance is a steady level kept up by beings arriving and leaving all the time.
explanations.description: In the Leaky Bottle, water ran in from the tap and out through a hole the whole time. Yet the level stayed at one mark. When you held the hole shut for a while, the level rose. When you let go, the deeper water pushed out faster, and the level came back down. A population works in a similar way. When there are more deer, each one finds less food, illness spreads more easily and predators catch them more often. So more deer die, and the number comes back down. This pushing back is called feedback. When you opened a second hole, the level settled at a new, lower mark. A lasting change, such as a new predator or a lost forest, moves the balance to a new level.
examples: In the Leaky Bottle, the level settled at one mark with one hole. With two holes it settled at a much lower mark.
With no hole at all the bottle overflows. Deer with no predators can multiply until they eat down their own food.
Numbers in nature are never perfectly still. They rise and fall within a range.
explanations.art: A clear plastic bottle under a thin stream from a tap, with one jet of water leaving a hole near the base and a pencil mark at the steady water level.

explanations.concept: Why prey animals have many young
explanations.definition: Think of a population that stays the same size. On average, each pair of parents is replaced by just two young who live to become parents. All the other young die first, and most of them are eaten.
explanations.description: A female Indian bullfrog lays thousands of eggs in one season. If all of them lived, ponds would overflow with frogs within a few years. They do not. So nearly all the eggs and tadpoles must be dying, most of them as food for fish, birds and snakes. An animal who is eaten often needs many young, so that two are still left. An animal who is seldom eaten, such as a tiger or an elephant, has few young. The mother looks after each one for years. So the number of young shows how dangerous life is for the young of that animal. It also shows how much of the web that animal feeds.
examples: A female rat can have 6 to 8 young at a time, several times a year. A tigress has 2 to 4 cubs every two or three years.
An elephant has one calf every few years, and the herd guards the calf.
In Two Out of Thousands, you coloured 2 squares for the frogs who live, out of 4,000 eggs.
explanations.art: A bullfrog beside a huge cloud of eggs in pond water, and a tigress walking with two cubs.

explanations.concept: Booms and crashes: eaters follow their food late
explanations.definition: When food increases, the number of eaters rises some time afterwards. When food runs short, the number of eaters falls some time afterwards. The delay makes numbers swing up and down.
explanations.description: In Ants and the Sugar Drop, the ants kept coming for several minutes after the sugar was gone. Populations show the same delay, over years. In northern Canada, fur traders kept records for about 200 years. They counted snowshoe hares and the lynx who hunt them. Hare numbers rise and crash about every ten years, and lynx numbers follow a year or two later. A sudden flood of food can also break a balance. In Mizoram, one kind of bamboo flowers and fruits all together about every 48 years. Rats feed on the fruit and multiply far faster than owls and snakes can. When the fruit is finished, the rats turn to the rice fields. People there call this mautam.
examples: In the Ten-Year Wave, the lynx line reached its top two years after the hare line.
The bamboo fruited in Mizoram in 1959, and again from 2006 to 2008. Both times, rats destroyed much of the rice crop.
Charles Elton and Mary Nicholson described the ten-year lynx cycle from the fur records in 1942.
explanations.art: A graph with two wavy lines, the hare line peaking first and the lynx line peaking just after, with a small hare and lynx drawn beside them.

explanations.concept: New arrivals: when a link is added
explanations.definition: An invasive species is a living being whom people bring to a new place. There they spread fast and harm the beings who already live there.
explanations.description: A web can be changed by adding a being as well as by removing one. In their old home, a plant or animal has eaters and illnesses that hold their numbers down. In a new place, those may be missing, so nothing pushes back. Lantana is a shrub from the Americas that was brought to India as a garden plant about 200 years ago. Deer and cattle avoid eating lantana, so lantana spreads and shades out the grass. Water hyacinth, from South America, covers ponds and lakes and blocks the light from the plants below. Most plants and animals that people carry to new places do not spread like this. Chilli, tomato and potato also came from the Americas, and they stay in the fields.
examples: In A New Arrival, adding lantana left less grass for the hare and the chital. That left less food for the dhole and the leopard.
A 2020 study found lantana in more than 40 of every 100 parts of India's tiger forests.
The Nile perch, a large hunting fish, was put into Lake Victoria in Africa in the 1950s. About 200 kinds of small fish found nowhere else then died out.
explanations.art: A lake covered edge to edge with green water hyacinth and purple flowers, with a fishing boat stuck among the plants.

explanations.concept: People in the web: hunting, cutting forests and protecting
explanations.definition: People are part of food webs. We change them by hunting, by cutting forests, by using poisons, and by protecting places and animals.
explanations.description: When people hunt out the carnivores, herbivores multiply and eat the plants down. Then the herbivores starve, and the whole web suffers. When a forest is cut, the producers go first, so every animal above them loses food and shelter. Bare ground also holds less rain, so floods and droughts become worse. India protects whole webs by law. The Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972 bans the hunting of protected animals. Project Tiger began in 1973. A tiger needs a large forest with many deer, so saving tigers saves everything below them. A national park has the strictest protection. A wildlife sanctuary also protects animals, but may allow some use, such as grazing. Long before these laws, the Bishnoi people of Rajasthan stood in front of trees to save them. So did the women of the Chipko movement.
examples: Mudumalai in Tamil Nadu, Periyar in Kerala, Kaziranga in Assam and Gir in Gujarat are protected forests.
Farmers in Tamil Nadu put up T-shaped perches in paddy fields. Owls sit on them and hunt rats at night.
India banned the cattle medicine diclofenac in 2006, because it was killing the vultures who ate dead cattle.
explanations.art: A T-shaped wooden perch standing in a paddy field at dusk with a barn owl sitting on it, and a forest hill behind.

explanations.concept: Does a web with more links stay steadier?
explanations.description: For a long time, ecologists thought that a web with many kinds and many links must be steadier. In 1972, Robert May tested this with mathematics and found the opposite for webs joined at random. Since then, scientists have looked for what makes real webs different from random ones. The answer seems to depend on what 'steady' means, and on how strong the links are.
examples: In the Two Webs Test, the wide web lost fewer beings. That test measures only one kind of steadiness: how many starve.
A field of one crop can be wiped out by one pest. A mixed forest seldom loses everything at once.

perspectives.explanation: More kinds and more links make a web steadier. If one food fails, eaters switch to another. Simple webs, such as islands and single-crop fields, suffer the worst outbreaks of pests.

In a mathematical web joined at random, more kinds and more links make the numbers swing more, not less. A disturbance has more paths to spread along. So links alone cannot be the reason real webs last.

perspectives.who: Kevin McCann and others (1998), Jennifer Dunne and others (2002)
perspectives.explanation: Real webs are not joined at random. Most of their links are weak, because most eaters take only a little of each food. Many weak links damp down the swings, and webs with more links lose fewer beings to hunger.

explanations.art: Three scientists' notebooks open side by side: one with a drawing of a rich forest, one full of equations, one with a food web drawn with thick and thin arrows.

explanations.concept: Why does the bamboo wait 48 years?
explanations.description: The bamboo called mautak covers the hills of Mizoram. Almost all the plants flower in the same few years, drop their fruit and die. Then the hills stay without bamboo fruit for about 48 years. In 1976 the ecologist Daniel Janzen suggested a reason. If a few plants fruited every year, rats and birds would eat nearly every seed. When all the plants fruit together, there is far more fruit than the eaters can finish. So many seeds are left to grow. The long wait keeps the numbers of seed eaters low in between. This idea fits what people see, but it is hard to test, because one test takes 48 years.
examples: Mango trees also fruit heavily in some years and lightly in others.
After the Mizoram bamboo fruited from 2006 to 2008, young bamboo came up thickly across the hills.
explanations.art: A hillside of tall bamboo covered in hanging green pear-shaped fruits, with a few rats on the ground among fallen fruit.

agreed.text: Every food web starts with producers, and most start with green plants or algae using sunlight.
agreed.evidence: No animal can make food from air and water. Trace any meal back, and the path ends at a plant or an alga. A few webs in the deep sea start with microbes that use chemicals instead of light.

agreed.text: Removing one kind of living being can change the numbers of many others, including beings they never eat.
agreed.evidence: Robert Paine removed starfish from a shore from the early 1960s and counted the animals for years. James Estes and John Palmisano compared islands with and without sea otters in 1974.

agreed.text: A population stays steady only when births and deaths roughly match.
agreed.evidence: Counts of animals over many years show numbers rising and falling within a range. When predators or food change, the range shifts.

agreed.text: Eaters with many foods cope with the loss of one food better than eaters with a single food.
agreed.evidence: In 2002, Jennifer Dunne and her team tested computer copies of real food webs. Webs with more links lost fewer further beings.

agreed.text: Living beings brought to new places by people can spread and harm the beings already there.
agreed.evidence: Records show the same pattern for the Nile perch in Lake Victoria, and for water hyacinth and lantana in India.

challenging.claim: Killing the snakes makes a village safer.
challenging.who: A common belief in many villages and towns
challenging.for: A few kinds of Indian snake have venom that can kill a person. Snakebite is a real danger for people who work in fields.
challenging.against: Most snakes near homes and fields are harmless rat snakes. Snakes eat rats, and rats eat stored grain and standing crops. Where snakes are killed, rats multiply. Knowing the few dangerous kinds and wearing shoes in the field protects people better.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that a village is better off with no snakes.

challenging.claim: Nature stays in perfect balance if people leave her alone.
challenging.who: A very old idea, found in many cultures
challenging.for: Forests and ponds can look the same for many years. Feedback does bring numbers back after small changes.
challenging.against: Counts over many years show numbers swinging widely even where no people live. Hares and lynx in Canada rise and crash about every ten years. Fires, floods and droughts also change webs.
challenging.context: This card is about whether nature has one fixed balance.

challenging.claim: A keystone species is always a big, fierce predator.
challenging.who: A common belief, because the best-known examples are wolves, tigers and sharks
challenging.for: The first keystone species to be named, a starfish, was a predator. Sea otters are predators too.
challenging.against: Fig trees, bees who pollinate, termites who build mounds and elephants who spread seeds can all be keystones. What counts is how much the web changes when they go.
challenging.context: This card is about what kinds of living beings can be keystone species.

challenging.claim: Poison is the best way to get rid of rats in a field.
challenging.for: Poison kills many rats quickly, and it is cheap.
challenging.against: Owls, snakes and cats who eat poisoned rats can die too. Rats breed much faster than their hunters, so the rats return first, with fewer hunters left. Traps, owl perches and clean grain stores work for longer.
challenging.context: This card is about using poison against rats, and what happens to the animals who eat rats.

challenging.claim: More links always make a food web safer.
challenging.who: Charles Elton and many ecologists before 1972
challenging.for: In the Two Webs Test and in computer tests on real webs, eaters with more foods starve less often.
challenging.against: Robert May showed in 1972 that in webs joined at random, more links make numbers swing more. Links also carry harm. A poison or a disease can spread along the same links as food.
challenging.context: This card is about whether having more links is always good for a web.

big_questions.q: A leopard never eats grass, yet leopards change how much grass grows. Who else changes your life without ever meeting you?
big_questions.hint: Think of who grew, carried and cooked your last meal, and who ate the pests on that farm.

big_questions.q: If numbers in nature keep rising and falling, is there such a thing as a balance of nature?
big_questions.hint: Think of the Leaky Bottle. The level was steady, but the water in the bottle was never the same water.

big_questions.q: A rat is a pest in a granary and food for an owl. Is being a pest a fact about the rat, or does it depend on who is looking?
big_questions.hint: Try describing the same rat as the owl would, then as the farmer would.

big_questions.q: Only two of a frog's thousands of young live to be parents. Were the other lives wasted?
big_questions.hint: Follow where the other tadpoles went. Who lived because of them?

big_questions.q: We can test a paper web in an hour, but a real forest takes many years. How much should we trust a model?
big_questions.hint: List what the Two Webs Test left out, and what it still got right.

big_questions.q: People have removed some beings from webs and added others. Should people now try to manage every web, or leave webs alone?
big_questions.hint: Think about the otters, the lantana and the owl perches. What did people know, and not know, each time?

story.title: The Year the Bamboo Flowered
story.note: Mautam is real. The bamboo of the Mizoram hills flowers and fruits all together about every 48 years. Rats multiplied and destroyed rice crops in 1959 and again from 2006 to 2008. The government did pay for rats' tails, and farmers were advised to grow ginger and turmeric. Zuali, Pi Thangi, Sanga and what their family did are made up. 'Pi' is a Mizo title of respect for an older woman.
text: In the spring of 2007, the bamboo on the hills around Zuali's village began to flower. Zuali was ten, and she had never seen bamboo flowers before. Nobody in her class had. Small pale tassels hung from every stem, on every slope, as far as she could see.
Her grandmother, Pi Thangi, looked at the hills for a long time. "Mautam," she said. "I was eleven the last time. It was 1959."
"What happened in 1959?" Zuali asked.
"The bamboo flowered. Then the rats came. Then there was no rice." Pi Thangi did not say more that day.

By the rains, the flowers had turned into fruit. They were green and as big as small pears, and they fell from the bamboo in thousands. Zuali's cousin Sanga, who was fourteen, cut one open. It was soft and pale inside. "Rats love these," he said. "Look how many there are already."

He was right. There were rats on the path, rats under the house, rats in the firewood. The government had promised a small reward for every rat's tail, and Sanga set traps each evening. At the end of the first week he had forty tails drying on a string. "Forty," he said. "At this speed I will finish them before the rice is ripe."

That night Zuali heard the barn owl who lived in the dead tree beside their field. She had raised three chicks that year. A rat snake lived under the granary too, and he was as long as Sanga was tall. Sanga had plans for both of them. The dead tree would make good firewood. And the snake, he said, frightened the hens.

Zuali sat on the bamboo floor with a piece of charcoal and began to draw. She drew a bamboo fruit and a rat, with an arrow from the fruit to the rat. She drew the owl and the snake, with arrows from the rat to each of them.
"Pi," she said, "how many babies does a rat have?"
"Six or seven at a time," said her grandmother. "When food is plenty, a mother has another family a few weeks later. And her daughters have their own before the season ends."

Zuali looked at her drawing. The owl had three chicks in one year. One rat mother might have twenty young before the rains ended, and those twenty would have young of their own. She looked at Sanga's string of forty tails. Then she looked out at the hills, where more fruit lay on the ground than all the rats in Mizoram could eat.
"Sanga," she said, "you cannot win. The fruit is making rats faster than you can trap them. Faster than the owl and the snake can eat them, too."
"Then I will trap harder," said Sanga.

Zuali did not answer. She was looking at the arrow from the fruit to the rat. Zuali did not answer. She was looking at the arrow from the fruit to the rat, and it worried her. The fruit would not lie there for ever. Already some of the fruits on the path had split, and a white root was pushing out of each one into the soil. Already some of the fruits on the path had split, and a white root was pushing out of each one into the soil.
"Pi," she said slowly, "when the fruit has all sprouted, what will the rats eat?"
Her grandmother put down her work.

Zuali drew a rice plant on the floor. She drew an arrow from the rice to the rat. "They are not here for our rice," she said. "They came for the fruit. But the fruit will be finished just when the rice is ripe. Then all of them will come to the fields at once."
"That is how it was," said Pi Thangi quietly. "They came in the night, like water running downhill. In the morning the field was stalks."
Nobody spoke. Then Zuali asked the question that mattered. "What will rats not eat?"
"Ginger," said her grandmother. "Turmeric. They leave those alone in the ground. The officer who came to the village said the same."

So that year the family did three things. They planted ginger and turmeric on half of their slope, and rice only on the other half. They packed last year's paddy into tin drums with tight lids. And when Sanga picked up his axe to cut the dead tree, Zuali stood in front of the trunk. "The owl catches rats every night for nothing," she said. "So does the snake. The fruit will finish one day, and then we will need every rat-catcher we have." Sanga looked at the charcoal arrows on the floor for a while. He put the axe away.

In October the rats came to the fields, just as the rice turned gold. The family banged tins and lit fires, but it made little difference. They saved three baskets of rice from half a slope. Many families saved less.

But the ginger and the turmeric lay safe under the soil, and the drums of old paddy stayed shut. The family sold ginger in the market at Aizawl and bought rice with the money. It was a hard year, and nobody in the house went hungry.

By the next spring there were few rats to be seen. Their food was gone, and most of them had starved. The old bamboo stood dry and dead on the hills, and beneath the dead stems the ground was green with young bamboo, thick as grass.

Zuali never rubbed out the drawing on the floor. Under the bamboo fruit she wrote a number in charcoal: 2055. "That is when it will flower again," she told Sanga. "I will be fifty-eight. Somebody will have to tell them what is coming."
story.epiphany: For the parent: the turn comes when Zuali adds a second arrow to her drawing. The rats and the rice were joined through the bamboo fruit. A flood of food at the bottom of the web made rats faster than any hunter could eat them. A rat has many young quickly, and an owl has few. When that food ended, the rats moved along another link, to the rice. Trapping could not undo this. Reading the web told the family what was coming and what to plant.
ask: Why could Sanga's traps not keep up with the rats?
The rats came for the bamboo fruit. Why did they end up in the rice fields?
Why did Zuali stop Sanga from cutting the owl's tree?
Why were there so few rats the next spring?
The bamboo will flower again in about 48 years. What would you tell the people living there then?

games.title: Up or Down?
games.context: This is a card game about following a change through a food web. Each card gives a food chain and one change. You say who becomes more and who becomes fewer, and why.

printables.title: 16 two-sided cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: Paddy → rat → rat snake. People kill the rat snakes. What happens to the rats? What happens to the paddy?
items.b: The rats become more, and the paddy becomes less. With fewer snakes, more rats live, and they eat more paddy.

items.f: Kelp → sea urchin → sea otter. Hunters kill almost all the sea otters. What happens to the urchins? What happens to the kelp?
items.b: The urchins become more, and the kelp becomes less. This really happened around islands in the North Pacific.

items.f: Starfish eat mussels. Mussels crowd other animals off the rock. A scientist removes the starfish. What happens to the mussels? What happens to the other animals?
items.b: The mussels become more, and the other animals become fewer. On Robert Paine's shore, the kinds of animals fell from 15 to 8.

items.f: Vultures and stray dogs both eat dead cattle. A cattle medicine kills most of the vultures. What happens to the dead cattle left lying? What happens to the dogs?
items.b: More dead cattle are left lying, and the dogs probably become more. This happened in India from the 1990s.

items.f: Bamboo fruit → rat. Rice → rat. All the bamboo fruits at once. What happens to the rats? When the fruit is finished, what happens to the rice?
items.b: The rats become more, and later the rice becomes less. People in Mizoram call this mautam.

items.f: Paddy → brown planthopper → spider. Insect poison kills the spiders. Some planthoppers live through it. What happens to the planthoppers later? What happens to the paddy?
items.b: The planthoppers become more, and the paddy becomes less. This has happened in paddy fields across Asia.

items.f: Crop insects → frog. People catch most of the frogs to sell. What happens to the insects? What happens to the crops?
items.b: The insects become more, and the crops become less. India stopped the export of frogs' legs in 1987.

items.f: Grass → chital → leopard. A disease kills most of the chital. What happens to the leopards? What happens to the grass?
items.b: The leopards become fewer, unless they find other prey. The grass becomes more.

items.f: Grass → hare. Lantana, a new shrub, shades out the grass. Hares do not eat lantana. What happens to the grass? What happens to the hares?
items.b: The grass becomes less, and the hares become fewer. A change at the bottom of a web passes upwards.

items.f: Small lake fish → Nile perch. The Nile perch, a big hunting fish, is put into a lake for the first time. What happens to the small fish?
items.b: The small fish become far fewer. In Lake Victoria, about 200 kinds of small fish died out.

items.f: Hare → lynx. The hares become many this year. What happens to the lynx? Does it happen this year or later?
items.b: The lynx become more, but a year or two later. Raising young takes time.

items.f: Paddy → rat → barn owl. A farmer puts up perches, and more owls come to hunt. What happens to the rats? What happens to the paddy?
items.b: The rats become fewer, and the paddy becomes more. Helping a predator can protect a crop.

items.f: Fig tree → barbet. Fig tree → langur. The fig trees in a forest are cut. What happens to the barbets? What happens to the langurs?
items.b: The barbets become fewer. The langurs also become fewer, though langurs can eat leaves too. A fig tree feeds many beings.

items.f: Paddy → rat → snake. Paddy → grasshopper → frog → snake. The snakes are killed. What happens to the paddy? Think about both paths.
items.b: It is hard to say. More rats eat more paddy. But more frogs eat more grasshoppers, which helps the paddy. Only counting in a real field can tell.

items.f: Grass → grasshopper → frog. A drought dries up the grass. What happens to the grasshoppers? What happens to the frogs?
items.b: The grasshoppers become fewer, and so do the frogs. Less food at the bottom means fewer eaters all the way up.

items.f: Fish → people. Fish → river dolphin. People catch far more fish than before. What happens to the fish? What happens to the dolphins?
items.b: The fish become fewer, and so do the dolphins. Two eaters who share one food affect each other.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, question side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. For each being the card asks about, say 'more' or 'fewer' and give a reason.
Turn the card over. Score 1 point for each being you got right with a reason.
If you got the whole card right, keep the card. If not, put it at the bottom of the pile.
Stop when every card has been read once. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: add up your points, then play again another day and try to beat your score.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Shuffle them and put them in a pile, question side up. 3. Remind everyone of the two rules. Fewer eaters means more of their food. Less food means fewer eaters.
flow.say: Each card changes one thing in a food chain. Our job is to say what happens next, and why. Remember the two rules.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Mix them. Put them in a pile, question side up. Remember the two rules.
flow.context: This is the first step of Up or Down? Here you set up the cards and recall the two rules for following a change.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read the top card aloud. 2. For each being asked about, say 'more' or 'fewer' and why. 3. Turn the card over and score 1 point for each right answer with a reason.
flow.say: Read the card aloud. Who becomes more? Who becomes fewer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Read the top card aloud. Say 'more' or 'fewer' for each being. Say why. Turn the card over. Score your points.

ask.q: Which cards start with a change at the top of the chain, and which at the bottom?
good: Killing snakes or otters starts at the top.
A drought or lantana shading the grass starts at the bottom.

flow.parent: A right answer needs a reason that names a link, such as 'because snakes eat rats'. Many of the cards are true stories, and the back says so.
flow.context: This is the main part of Up or Down? Here you read each card, say who becomes more and who becomes fewer, and check the back.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Look again at the cards that were got wrong. 3. Ask which true story on the cards was the most surprising.
flow.say: Which card fooled us? Which true story surprised you most?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which card fooled you? Which true story surprised you most?

check.q: Snakes eat rats and frogs. Rats eat paddy. Frogs eat grasshoppers, who eat paddy. The snakes are killed. What happens to the paddy?
options: The paddy must become more
The paddy must become less
It depends which path is stronger
check.why: One path pushes the paddy down, through more rats. The other pushes it up, through more frogs and fewer grasshoppers. A drawing cannot say which wins. Someone has to count in a real field.

flow.context: This is the last step of Up or Down? Here you count the points and talk about the cards that surprised you.

games.title: Which Box?
games.context: This is a quick sorting game. Each card names an animal or another living being and what they eat. You put the card in the right box: herbivore, carnivore, omnivore, scavenger or decomposer. Some cards fit two boxes.

printables.title: 20 two-sided cards to cut out (the box is on the back)

items.f: Chital deer. She eats grass, leaves and fallen fruit.
items.b: Herbivore. Everything she eats comes from plants.

items.f: Elephant. She eats grass, leaves, bark and fruit.
items.b: Herbivore. An elephant eats about 150 kilograms of plants a day.

items.f: Grasshopper. She eats the leaves of grasses and crops.
items.b: Herbivore. Small animals can be herbivores too.

items.f: Rose-ringed parakeet. She eats fruit, seeds and grain.
items.b: Herbivore. Fruit, seeds and grain are all parts of plants.

items.f: Tiger. She eats deer and wild pigs.
items.b: Carnivore. She eats only other animals.

items.f: Frog. She eats flies, mosquitoes and grasshoppers.
items.b: Carnivore. Insects are animals, so an insect-eater is a carnivore.

items.f: House cat. She eats mice, small birds and lizards.
items.b: Carnivore. A cat's body needs meat.

items.f: Rat snake. He eats rats, frogs and lizards.
items.b: Carnivore. He swallows his prey whole.

items.f: Barn owl. She eats rats and mice.
items.b: Carnivore. She hunts at night by listening.

items.f: Human. We eat rice, dal, vegetables, fruit, milk, eggs, fish and meat.
items.b: Omnivore. Humans can live on many mixes of plant and animal food.

items.f: Crow. She eats grain, fruit, insects, eggs, kitchen scraps and dead animals.
items.b: Two boxes: omnivore and scavenger. A crow eats almost anything.

items.f: Sloth bear. He eats termites, ants, honey and fruit.
items.b: Omnivore. Termites and ants are animals. Honey and fruit come from plants.

items.f: Peafowl. She eats seeds, berries, insects and small lizards.
items.b: Omnivore. She eats both plants and animals.

items.f: Vulture. She eats the bodies of animals who have died.
items.b: Scavenger. She does not kill her food.

items.f: Striped hyena. He eats mostly dead animals and bones.
items.b: Scavenger. His jaws can crack large bones.

items.f: Golden jackal. He hunts small animals, eats fruit and feeds on dead animals.
items.b: Two boxes: omnivore and scavenger.

items.f: Black kite. She catches small animals and also eats dead ones.
items.b: Two boxes: carnivore and scavenger.

items.f: Mushroom on a rotting log. The fungus feeds on the dead wood.
items.b: Decomposer. The fungus breaks dead wood down into simple matter.

items.f: Mould on old bread. The fungus feeds on the bread.
items.b: Decomposer. Mould is a fungus that digests food outside their body.

items.f: Earthworm. She eats dead leaves in the soil.
items.b: Decomposer box. She breaks dead leaves into small pieces, and fungi and bacteria finish the work.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, animal side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say which box the card belongs in, and why.
Turn the card over. Score 1 point for the right box.
If the back says 'two boxes', score 2 points if you named both.
Put the card on its box on the mat. If it fits two boxes, lay it across both.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most points wins. Playing alone, try to beat your last score.

setup.art: A paper mat with five labelled boxes in a row and a pile of small cards beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the mat with five boxes and the pile of cards.

setup.art: A child holding a card that says 'Frog' and placing the card on the Carnivore box.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card, choose a box and say why.

setup.art: A card that says 'Crow' lying across the line between the Omnivore and Scavenger boxes.
setup.caption: 3. A card that fits two boxes lies across both.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards and the mat. 2. Shuffle the cards. 3. Read the five box names aloud.
flow.say: There are five ways to get food. Let's see where each of these beings belongs.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and the mat. Mix the cards. Read the five box names.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Box? Here you set up the cards and the mat with five boxes.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read the top card. 2. Say the box and the reason. 3. Turn the card over, score, and place the card on the mat.
flow.say: What does this one eat? So which box? Could this one fit a second box too?
flow.kid: Read the card. Say the box. Say why. Turn it over. Put the card on the mat.
flow.parent: A good reason uses what the card says the being eats. If your child puts the frog with the herbivores, ask whether a fly is a plant or an animal.
flow.context: This is the main part of Which Box? Here you sort each being by what they eat.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Look at the cards lying across two boxes. 3. Ask why some animals do not fit in one box.
flow.say: Three cards lie across two boxes. Why don't these animals fit in one?
flow.kid: Count your points. Look at the cards across two boxes. Why don't they fit in one?

ask.q: Why do some animals fit two boxes?
good: They get food in more than one way.
The boxes are our words. Animals eat whatever they can find.

check.q: A frog eats flies, mosquitoes and grasshoppers. Which box fits a frog?
options: Herbivore, because a frog is small
Carnivore, because insects are animals
Scavenger, because flies are dirty
check.why: A carnivore eats other animals, and insects are animals. The box does not depend on size. A grasshopper is small and a herbivore, and a frog is small and a carnivore.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which Box? Here you count the points and talk about the animals who fit two boxes.

experiments.title: The Two Webs Test: which web loses more when three beings go?
experiments.context: In this experiment you draw two paper food webs of the same forest. In the narrow web each animal eats one food. In the wide web most animals eat several. You take the same three beings out of both and count who is left.
experiments.question: Two webs have the same 10 beings. When the same 3 beings disappear from both, which web has more beings left: the one with 7 links or the one with 18 links?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Three beings will be taken from both webs. Will the narrow web or the wide web have more beings left, or will they be the same? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Both webs have the same 10 beings. In each round, the same 3 beings are taken from both webs. Only the number of arrows is different. Play 6 rounds, because one draw of cards can be a fluke.

materials.item: sheets of plain paper, A4 size or bigger (old calendar pages work well)
a pencil and a ruler
small things to use as tokens, such as coins, buttons or dry chana
small slips of paper for name cards
a steel bowl or tumbler to shake the name cards in

schedule.what: Draw the narrow web and the wide web. Guess. Play 6 rounds of taking 3 beings away. Find the averages and explain them.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for 6 rounds. Find the average number left in each web, and draw two bars. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: average number of beings left out of 10
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Two sheets of paper side by side, each with the same ten names in four rows: grass, shrubs and fig tree at the bottom, then grasshopper, hare, chital and langur, then peafowl, then dhole and leopard at the top. The left sheet has 7 arrows and the right sheet has 18.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the same 10 beings on two sheets. Draw 7 arrows on one and 18 on the other.

setup.art: A child's hand drawing three folded paper slips out of a steel bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Draw 3 name cards. Take those beings off both webs.

setup.art: The two paper webs with coins on the names. On the left sheet five names have no coin, on the right sheet only three.
setup.caption: 3. Take off any animal with no food left. Count who remains.

flow.do: 1. On both sheets, write the same 10 names in the same places. Bottom row: Grass, Shrubs, Fig tree. Second row: Grasshopper, Hare, Chital, Langur. Third row: Peafowl. Top row: Dhole, Leopard. 2. On sheet 1, write NARROW WEB. Here each animal eats one food. The grasshopper and the hare eat grass. The chital eats shrubs. The langur eats figs. The peafowl eats grasshoppers. The dhole eats hares. The leopard eats chital. 3. On sheet 2, write WIDE WEB. The grasshopper and the hare eat grass and shrubs. The chital eats grass, shrubs and figs. The langur eats shrubs and figs. The peafowl eats grass seeds, figs and grasshoppers. The dhole eats hares and chital. The leopard eats hares, chital, langurs and peafowl. 4. Draw an arrow from each food to the eater. Count the arrows.
flow.say: These are beings of the Mudumalai forest in Tamil Nadu. A chital is a spotted deer, and a dhole is a wild dog. Let's draw the same forest twice. In one web each animal eats one food. In the other, most animals eat several.
flow.kid: Write the same 10 names on two sheets. On sheet 1, each animal eats one food. On sheet 2, most animals eat several foods. Draw an arrow from each food to the eater. Count the arrows on each sheet.
flow.parent: Sheet 1 should have 7 arrows and sheet 2 should have 18. The wide web is close to what these animals really eat. The narrow web is made up for the test. No real leopard eats only chital.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two Webs Test. Here you draw two food webs of the same forest, one with 7 arrows and one with 18.

flow.do: 1. Put one token on every name on both sheets. 2. Write the 10 names on 10 slips of paper and fold them. 3. Explain that 3 beings will be taken from both webs. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write them down.
flow.say: We will take the same three beings away from both webs. Which web will have more beings left afterwards? Or will they be the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put a token on every name. Three beings will be taken from both webs. Which web will have more left? Why? Write your guess.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: In the wide web an animal can eat something else if one food goes.
They will be the same, because both lose 3 beings. (A fair guess. The test will show.)

flow.context: This step of the Two Webs Test is for guessing. You guess which web will have more beings left when three are taken away, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Teach the hunger rule on the narrow web. Take the token off Hare. 2. Ask who eats only hares in this web. Take the token off Dhole too. 3. Say the rule: an animal with no food left in the web is lost. 4. Put both tokens back.
flow.say: Here is the hunger rule. When a being goes, look at everyone who eats them. If an animal has no food left, that animal is lost too. Then check again, because the loss can pass further up.
flow.kid: Take the token off Hare on the narrow web. Who eats only hares? Take that token off too. An animal with no food left is lost. Put the tokens back.
flow.parent: Plants need no food from the web, so a plant is lost only when their own card is drawn. Keep checking until nobody else is without food.
flow.context: This step of the Two Webs Test teaches the hunger rule. An animal is lost when every food they eat has gone from the web.

flow.do: 1. Shake the 10 name cards in the bowl and draw 3. 2. Take the tokens off those 3 beings on both sheets. 3. On each sheet, use the hunger rule until nobody else is lost. 4. Count the tokens left on each sheet and write both numbers in the table. 5. Put all the tokens and cards back. 6. Play 6 rounds.
flow.say: Draw three cards. Those three beings are gone from both forests. Now check each animal on each sheet. Does she still have a food with a token on it?
flow.kid: Shake the cards and draw 3. Take those tokens off both sheets. Take off any animal with no food left. Check again. Count the tokens left on each sheet. Write the numbers. Play 6 rounds.

ask.q: Which card did the most harm in the narrow web when it was drawn?
good: Grass, because the grasshopper, hare, peafowl and dhole all depended on grass.
A plant card, because everything above the plant went too.

flow.parent: The wide web can never have fewer left than the narrow web. It has every arrow of the narrow web, and more. Most rounds leave 6 or 7 in the wide web and 3 to 7 in the narrow web. In about one round in six they tie. If all three plant cards come out together, both webs lose everyone.
flow.context: This is the main step of the Two Webs Test. In each of 6 rounds you take the same 3 beings from both webs and count who is left.

flow.do: 1. Add up the 6 numbers for the narrow web and divide by 6. Do the same for the wide web. 2. Draw two bars to compare the averages. 3. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 4. Ask what the paper model leaves out.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Find the average for each web. Draw two bars. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: Why did the wide web lose fewer beings?
good: Most animals there had another food left when one food went.
In the narrow web each animal had only one food, so one loss passed up the chain.

ask.q: Our model follows hunger only. What could happen in a real forest that the model leaves out?
good: If the leopard and dhole go, the chital could multiply and eat down the plants.
Animals can move away or find new foods.
Some links are strong and some are weak.

check.q: In the Two Webs Test, why were more beings left in the wide web?
options: The wide web had more beings to start with
Most eaters there had another food to turn to
Fewer cards were drawn for the wide web
check.why: Both webs had 10 beings and lost the same 3 cards, so the test was fair. The difference was the arrows. An eater with several foods still has something to eat when one food goes. Choosing the first answer means forgetting that both webs started with the same 10.

flow.context: This step of the Two Webs Test works out the results. You find the average number of beings left in each web and explain the difference.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to add just one new arrow to the narrow web, where they think it will help most. 2. Ask why they chose that place. 3. Play 3 more rounds on the narrow web and see if the average rises.
flow.say: Now you change the test. You may add one arrow to the narrow web. Where will one new link help the most? Why there?
flow.kid: Add one new arrow to the narrow web. Choose where it helps most. Say why. Play 3 more rounds.
flow.parent: A strong choice gives a second food to an animal near the bottom, such as shrubs to the hare. Then the loss of grass no longer starves so many. Three rounds are too few to be sure, and that is worth saying aloud.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Two Webs Test. Here you add one arrow of your own to the narrow web and test whether it helps.

experiments.title: The Leaky Bottle: what keeps a level steady?
experiments.context: In this experiment a thin stream of tap water runs into a bottle with a hole near the base. It is a model of a population, where births add and deaths take away. You find out what the water level does.
experiments.question: Water runs into a bottle and out through a hole at the same time. Does the level keep rising, keep falling, or stop at one height? What does a second hole do?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When water runs in at the top and out at the hole, what will the level do? Then guess what will happen to the level if you open a second hole of the same size. Why do you think so? Write both guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same bottle and the same tap all through. Once the stream is set, do not touch the tap again. Only one thing changes at a time: first a finger over the hole for a count of 30, then a second hole.

materials.item: a clear 1-litre plastic bottle with straight sides, cap off
a thick nail and pliers, or the point of a compass, for the grown-up
strong sticky tape, such as brown packing tape
a ruler and a marker pen
a bucket to stand the bottle in and catch the water
a tap in a bathroom or at a sink
a clock or phone timer

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the holes. A heated nail is very hot, so hold it with pliers and keep children back. Do the test in a bathroom or at a sink, because wet floors are slippery.

schedule.what: Make the bottle. Guess. Let the level settle with one hole. Cover the hole for a count of 30 and watch the level return. Open the second hole and find the new level.

experiments.record: Write the level every minute in the table. Draw a line graph of level against minutes. Mark where you covered the hole and where you opened the second hole. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: water level in the Leaky Bottle
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished graph can look like. The hole was covered for a count of 30 just before minute 9. The second hole was opened at minute 13. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A clear plastic bottle with two small holes near the base on opposite sides, one covered with brown tape, and marker lines every centimetre up the side.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes two small holes, 3 cm above the base. Tape one shut. Mark every centimetre.

setup.art: The bottle standing in a bucket under a tap, a thin stream of water going into its mouth and a thin jet leaving the open hole.
setup.caption: 2. Let a thin, steady stream run in. Read the level every minute.

setup.art: The same bottle with the tape peeled off, two jets of water leaving, and the water level much lower than an earlier pen mark.
setup.caption: 3. Open the second hole and find the new level.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up makes two holes in the bottle, each about 3 mm wide, as wide as a matchstick. Both are 3 cm above the base, on opposite sides. 2. Dry the bottle. Press tape firmly over one hole. 3. With the ruler and marker, draw a line every 1 cm up the side. Start with 0 level with the holes and go up to 18.
flow.say: This bottle is our model. Water coming in will stand for animals being born. Water going out will stand for animals dying. The level will stand for how many animals there are.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes two small holes near the base. Tape one hole shut. Draw a line every centimetre up the side. Start at the holes.
flow.parent: A nail heated on the gas flame for a few seconds and held with pliers melts a neat hole. Make both holes the same size. The tape must go on while the bottle is dry, or it will not hold.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Leaky Bottle. Here a grown-up makes two small holes near the base, and you mark a scale on the side.

flow.do: 1. Show how the test will work, without turning on the tap. 2. Ask what the level will do when water runs in and out together. 3. Ask what a second hole will do to the level. 4. Write down both guesses and the reasons.
flow.say: Water will run in at the top and out at the hole. What will the level do? Later we will open a second hole. What will the level do then? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Water will run in and out together. What will the level do? What will a second hole do? Say why. Write your guesses.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: It will stop where the water going out equals the water coming in.
With two holes the level will be half as high. (A fair guess. The test will show.)

flow.context: This step of the Leaky Bottle is for guessing. You guess what the water level will do with one hole, and then with two.

flow.do: 1. Stand the bottle in the bucket under the tap. 2. Open the tap to a thin, steady stream that goes into the mouth of the bottle. 3. Read the level every minute for 8 minutes and write it down. 4. When the level stays the same for 2 minutes, mark it with the pen.
flow.say: Read the level each minute. Is it still rising? Is it rising as fast as before?
flow.kid: Stand the bottle under the tap. Let a thin stream run in. Read the level every minute. Mark where it stops rising.

ask.q: The level has stopped, but water is still running in. Where is that water going?
good: Out of the hole, just as fast as it comes in.

flow.parent: You want the level to settle between 8 and 16 cm. If the water reaches the shoulder of the bottle, turn the tap down a little and start the readings again. If it settles below 6 cm, turn the tap up a little. After that, do not touch the tap. The test uses about one bucket of water, so keep it for mopping or for plants.
flow.context: This step of the Leaky Bottle lets water run in from the tap and out through one hole. You read the level each minute until it stops changing.

flow.do: 1. Press a finger firmly over the open hole for a slow count of 30. 2. Let go, and read the level at once. 3. Read the level every minute for 4 minutes.
flow.say: Now nothing can leave for a short while. What will the level do? And what will it do when you let go?
flow.kid: Press a finger on the hole. Count slowly to 30. Let go. Read the level every minute for 4 minutes.

ask.q: The level came back to the old mark. Look at the jet. What was different while the level was high?
good: The jet shot out farther and faster.
Deeper water pushes out faster, so the extra water drained away.

flow.parent: The level should rise 3 to 4 cm and then sink back to the pen mark within about 4 minutes. This return is the feedback. Do not explain it yet. Ask what your child noticed about the jet.
flow.context: This step of the Leaky Bottle blocks the hole for a count of 30, so the level rises. Then you watch whether the level comes back to the old mark.

flow.do: 1. Peel the tape off the second hole. 2. Read the level every minute for 5 minutes. 3. Mark the new steady level with the pen. 4. Measure both pen marks from the holes.
flow.say: Now water can leave by two holes. Watch the level. Where does it stop this time?
flow.kid: Peel the tape off the second hole. Read the level every minute. Mark where it stops. Measure both marks.
flow.parent: With two equal holes the level usually settles at about a quarter of the first height, not a half. A jet from deep water is faster than a jet from shallow water, but not by much. So the level has to fall a long way before two slow jets carry what one fast jet did. If your result is nearer a third, the holes are probably not quite equal.
flow.context: This step of the Leaky Bottle opens a second hole. You find the new, lower level where the water settles.

flow.do: 1. Turn off the tap. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 3. Then match the model to a herd of deer. Ask what the tap, the holes and the level stand for.
flow.say: Tell me what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Then tell me what the tap, the hole and the level would be in a herd of deer.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Then say what the tap, the hole and the level stand for.

ask.q: In a herd of deer, what is like the second hole?
good: A new predator, a disease or hunters: one more way for deer to die.

ask.q: With no hole at all, the bottle would overflow. What is that like in a forest?
good: Deer with no predators multiply until they eat down their own food.

check.q: In the Leaky Bottle, why did the level stay at one mark?
options: The water stopped moving
Water left as fast as it arrived
The bottle was full
check.why: Water kept running in and out the whole time. The level stayed still because the two flows were equal. Choosing 'the water stopped moving' means thinking that a steady number needs nothing to change. In nature too, a steady number hides births and deaths going on all the time.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Leaky Bottle. Here you explain why the level settled, and match the bottle to a population of deer.

experiments.title: Ants and the Sugar Drop: how fast do eaters follow their food?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put a drop of sugar water where ants walk. You count the ants every 2 minutes as they gather. Then you take the sugar away and keep counting.
experiments.question: When food appears, how quickly does the number of ants rise? When the food is taken away, how quickly does the number fall?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Sketch how you think the number of ants will change over 16 minutes. Then guess how many minutes the ants will stay after the sugar is taken away. Why do you think so? Write your guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Count only the ants inside the circle. Count every 2 minutes by the clock. Do not move the paper, blow on the ants or add more sugar during the test.
results_table: Minutes since the first ant arrived

materials.item: sugar
water
a sheet of white paper with a circle 10 cm across drawn on it (draw round a steel tumbler or a small bowl)
a small square of paper, about 3 cm across, to hold the sugar
a clock or phone timer, a pencil and squared paper for the graph

schedule.what: Put the sugar where ants walk. Count the ants every 2 minutes for 16 minutes. Take the sugar away and count for 10 more minutes. Draw the graph.

experiments.record: Write the count every 2 minutes in the table. Draw a line graph of ants against minutes, and mark the minute when you took the sugar away. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: ants inside the circle
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished graph can look like. The sugar was taken away at minute 16. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A sheet of white paper on a kitchen floor near a wall, with a pencil circle on it and a small square of paper holding a wet patch of sugar in the middle. A line of ants walks nearby.
setup.caption: 1. Put the paper where ants walk, with wet sugar in the middle of the circle.

setup.art: A child crouching beside the paper with a phone timer, counting about twenty ants inside the circle.
setup.caption: 2. Count the ants inside the circle every 2 minutes.

setup.art: The same paper with the small sugar square lifted away, and ants still walking about inside the circle.
setup.caption: 3. Take the sugar away. Keep counting for 10 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Find a place where ants walk, such as a window sill, a balcony floor or a kitchen corner. 2. Lay the sheet of paper there, with the circle facing up. 3. Mix the sugar with the drops of water on the small square. 4. Put the square in the middle of the circle.
flow.say: We are putting out a small feast. Let's see who finds it, and how fast the news spreads.
flow.kid: Find where ants walk. Lay the paper there. Wet the sugar on the small square. Put it in the middle of the circle.
flow.parent: The first ant may take 5 to 30 minutes to find the sugar. Do something else nearby while you wait. If no ant has come in 30 minutes, move the paper close to where you last saw ants. Or try again in the evening. Small black or red house ants work well. Do not use big red tree ants, who bite hard.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ants and the Sugar Drop. Here you put wet sugar on a paper circle where ants walk.

flow.do: 1. While you wait for the first ant, ask for a guess. 2. Ask your child to sketch how the number of ants will change over 16 minutes. 3. Ask how long the ants will stay once the sugar is gone, and why.
flow.say: How do you think the number of ants will change? Will it rise steadily, or slowly at first? When we take the sugar away, how soon will they leave? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Sketch how the number of ants will change. When the sugar goes, how soon will they leave? Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: One ant finds the sugar first and the others follow her, so the number rises slowly at first.
They will leave at once because there is nothing to eat. (A fair guess. The test will show.)

flow.context: This step of Ants and the Sugar Drop is for guessing. You guess how the number of ants will rise, and how soon they will leave when the sugar is gone.

flow.do: 1. When the first ant reaches the sugar, start the timer. Write 1 ant at 0 minutes. 2. Every 2 minutes, count the ants inside the circle and write the number. 3. Go on for 16 minutes.
flow.say: The first ant is here. Start the clock. Every two minutes, count everyone inside the circle.
flow.kid: Start the timer when the first ant arrives. Count the ants in the circle every 2 minutes. Write each number. Go on for 16 minutes.

ask.q: How do the later ants know where to come?
good: The first ants lay a scent trail on the way home, and the others follow the scent.

flow.parent: If there are too many to count one by one, count one half of the circle and double it. The numbers usually rise slowly for a few minutes and then quickly.
flow.context: In this step of Ants and the Sugar Drop the sugar is there. You count the ants every 2 minutes for 16 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Lift the small square with the sugar off the paper. Tap it gently so the ants on it drop back into the circle. 2. Put the square far away, in another room. 3. Go on counting the ants inside the circle every 2 minutes for 10 minutes.
flow.say: The food is gone now. Keep counting. Do the ants know yet?
flow.kid: Lift the sugar square away. Tap the ants off gently. Count the ants in the circle every 2 minutes. Go on for 10 minutes.
flow.parent: New ants usually keep arriving for several minutes, because the scent trail is still there. The count falls slowly, not all at once. Afterwards, put the sugar square outside for the ants.
flow.context: This step of Ants and the Sugar Drop takes the sugar away. You keep counting, to see how soon the ants leave.

flow.do: 1. Draw a line graph of the number of ants against minutes. 2. Mark the minute when the sugar was taken away. 3. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened.
flow.say: Look at your graph. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Draw your line graph. Mark when the sugar went. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: Owls and snakes eat rats. If rats suddenly had far more food, would the owls and snakes multiply at once?
good: No. Their numbers would rise later, because raising young takes time.
The eaters follow the food late, as the ants did.

check.q: In Ants and the Sugar Drop, what happened after the sugar was taken away?
options: All the ants left at once
Ants kept coming for some minutes
The number of ants doubled
check.why: The scent trail to the sugar was still there, so ants went on following it for a while. The number fell slowly. The number of eaters follows the food, but late. Choosing 'left at once' means expecting no delay.

flow.context: This is the last step of Ants and the Sugar Drop. Here you draw the graph and explain why the ants stayed after the sugar was gone.

activities.title: Chain to Web: count the arrows
activities.context: This short activity starts the unit. You take one food chain and add what each animal really eats, until the chain becomes a food web. Then you count the links.

materials.item: a sheet of paper
a pencil and a colour pencil

activities.record: Keep your web drawing. Write the number of beings and the number of arrows under it.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a straight chain written across it: grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, eagle, joined by four arrows.
setup.caption: 1. Write one food chain and count the arrows.

setup.art: The same sheet with a rat, a lizard, a fly, paddy and a myna added, and many crossing arrows in another colour.
setup.caption: 2. Add what each animal really eats. Count the arrows again.

flow.do: 1. Write this chain across the middle of the paper: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle. 2. Ask what each arrow means. 3. Count the beings and the arrows.
flow.say: Here is a food chain from a field. What does an arrow mean? How many beings are there, and how many arrows?
flow.kid: Write the chain: grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, eagle. Draw the arrows. Count the beings. Count the arrows.
flow.parent: An arrow means 'is eaten by'. It points the way the food goes. There are 5 beings and 4 arrows.
flow.context: This is the first step of Chain to Web. Here you write one food chain from a field and count the arrows.

flow.do: 1. Point to each animal in turn. Ask what else she eats, and who else eats her. 2. Write each new being on the paper. 3. Draw every new arrow in colour, from the food to the eater. 4. Add at least 5 new beings.
flow.say: Does a frog eat only grasshoppers? Does a snake eat only frogs? Let's add what each one really eats.
flow.kid: Look at each animal. What else does she eat? Who else eats her? Add 5 new beings. Draw the new arrows in colour.
flow.parent: Some true links to offer if your child is stuck: a frog also eats flies. A snake also eats rats and lizards. An eagle also eats rats and lizards. A rat eats grass seeds and paddy. A lizard and a myna eat grasshoppers. A grasshopper also eats paddy leaves.
flow.context: This step of Chain to Web adds what each animal in the chain really eats. The chain grows into a web.

flow.do: 1. Count all the beings and all the arrows now. 2. Divide the arrows by the beings. 3. Ask what the web shows that the chain did not.
flow.say: How many arrows are there now? What can you see in the web that the chain was hiding?
flow.kid: Count the beings. Count the arrows. Divide arrows by beings. What does the web show that the chain hid?

ask.q: What does the web show that the chain did not?
good: Most animals have more than one food.
If the frogs went, the snake could still eat rats.
One animal can be in many chains at once.

flow.context: This is the last step of Chain to Web. Here you count the links in your web and say what a web shows that a chain hides.

activities.title: Take the Snakes Away: follow a change through a web
activities.context: In this activity you draw a small food web of a paddy field. You take the rat snakes away and follow the change step by step. Coins show who becomes more and who becomes fewer.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil
coins

activities.record: Write the steps as a chain of changes, such as: snakes gone → rats more → paddy less.

setup.art: A hand-drawn web with six names: paddy at the bottom, grasshopper and rat above, frog above grasshopper, and rat snake and owl at the top, joined by six arrows.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the paddy field web with 6 beings and 6 arrows.

setup.art: The same web with the rat snake crossed out, a coin showing heads on rat and frog, and a coin showing tails on grasshopper.
setup.caption: 2. Cross out the snake. Heads means more, tails means fewer.

flow.do: 1. Write six names: Paddy, Grasshopper, Rat, Frog, Rat snake, Owl. 2. Draw six arrows. Paddy goes to the grasshopper and to the rat. The grasshopper goes to the frog. The frog and the rat go to the rat snake. The rat also goes to the owl. 3. Teach the two rules.
flow.say: Here are two rules. When an eater becomes fewer, their food becomes more. When a food becomes fewer, their eaters become fewer too.
flow.kid: Draw the six beings and six arrows. Learn two rules. Fewer eaters means more of their food. Less food means fewer eaters.
