flow.parent: The rules also work the other way round. More eaters means less of their food, and more food means more eaters.
flow.context: This is the first step of Take the Snakes Away. Here you draw the web of a paddy field and learn two rules for following a change.

flow.do: 1. Cross out the rat snake. Ask who is changed first, and how. Put a coin heads up for 'more' and tails up for 'fewer'. 2. Ask who is changed next. 3. Go on until every being has a coin. 4. Ask what happens to the paddy.
flow.say: People have killed the rat snakes. Who feels it first? Will there be more of them, or fewer? Why? Who feels it next?
flow.kid: Cross out the snake. Who changes first? Heads means more. Tails means fewer. Go on until every being has a coin.

ask.q: What happens to the paddy?
good: More rats eat more paddy, so the paddy goes down.
More frogs eat more grasshoppers, so the paddy is eaten less by grasshoppers. The two paths push opposite ways.

flow.parent: Step one: rats become more and frogs become more. Step two: more rats eat more paddy, more frogs eat more grasshoppers, and more rats can feed more owls later. Step three: fewer grasshoppers eat less paddy. So the paddy is pushed down by one path and up by another. Farmers' experience is that the rats win, and the harvest falls.
flow.context: This is the main step of Take the Snakes Away. You remove the rat snakes from the paddy field web and follow the change from being to being.

flow.do: 1. Take the coins off and bring the snake back. 2. Ask your child to choose a different change, such as catching all the frogs or putting up an owl perch. 3. Ask them to follow it through with the coins. 4. Ask which effects are direct and which are indirect.
flow.say: Now you choose the change. Follow it through the web. Which effect is direct, along one arrow? Which is indirect, through someone in between?
flow.kid: Bring the snake back. Choose a new change. Follow it with the coins. Which effects are direct? Which are indirect?

check.q: People kill the rat snakes in a paddy field. Which is a direct effect?
options: The rats become more
The paddy becomes less
The grasshoppers become fewer
check.why: Snakes eat rats, so losing the snakes acts on the rats along one arrow. That is direct. The paddy and the grasshoppers change too, but only through the rats or the frogs in between. Those effects are indirect.

flow.context: This is the last step of Take the Snakes Away. Here you choose a change of your own and sort the effects into direct and indirect.

activities.title: Two Out of Thousands: why prey animals have many young
activities.context: The number of frogs in a pond stays about the same. In this activity you work out how many of a frog's young can live to be parents. You colour squares to compare a frog with a tigress.

materials.item: a page from a squared maths notebook
a pencil, a ruler and two colour pencils

activities.record: Keep the page. Under each drawing write the share who live, such as '2 in 4,000'.

setup.art: A squared notebook page with a box of 10 by 10 small squares drawn on it, labelled '100 eggs', and a note '40 boxes like this'.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a box of 100 squares. It stands for 100 frog eggs.

setup.art: The same page with two small squares coloured green in the box, and beside it a row of 12 squares with two coloured orange.
setup.caption: 2. Colour the 2 who live. Do the same for a tigress's 12 cubs.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that a pair of bullfrogs may leave about 4,000 eggs in their lives. 2. Say that the number of frogs in their pond stays about the same from year to year. 3. Ask how many of the 4,000 can live to be parents.
flow.say: A pair of frogs leaves about 4,000 eggs. The pond has about the same number of frogs every year. So how many of those 4,000 grow up to be parents? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two frogs leave 4,000 eggs. The pond keeps the same number of frogs. How many of the 4,000 become parents? Say why.
flow.parent: The answer is about 2. Two parents are replaced by two young. If 3 lived, the frogs would grow by half in every generation. Let your child reason it out. Do not give the answer yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Out of Thousands. Here you ask how many of a frog pair's 4,000 eggs can live to be parents.

flow.do: 1. Draw a box 10 squares wide and 10 squares tall. It holds 100 squares, for 100 eggs. 2. Work out how many such boxes make 4,000 eggs. 3. Colour 2 squares for the young who live. 4. Next to it, draw 12 squares for the cubs a tigress may have in her life. Colour 2.
flow.say: One box is 100 eggs. How many boxes would we need for 4,000? Only two squares in all those boxes get coloured.
flow.kid: Draw a box of 100 squares. You would need 40 boxes for 4,000 eggs. Colour 2 squares. Now draw 12 squares for a tigress. Colour 2.

ask.q: What share of the frog's young live? What share of the tigress's?
good: 2 in 4,000, which is 1 in 2,000.
2 in 12, which is 1 in 6.

flow.context: This step of Two Out of Thousands colours squares. They compare how many young live for a frog and for a tigress.

flow.do: 1. Ask where the other 3,998 went. 2. Ask who was fed by them. 3. Ask why a frog needs so many young and a tigress needs so few.
flow.say: Where did the other 3,998 go? Who ate them? Why does a frog lay thousands of eggs, when a tigress has two or three cubs?
flow.kid: Where did the other 3,998 go? Who ate them? Why does a frog need so many young?

check.q: Why do animals who are eaten often have many young?
options: So that a few are still left to become parents
Because they are small
Because they like big families
check.why: Most of the young of a prey animal are eaten before they grow up. With many young, a few are still left. Small size is not the reason. A sparrow is small, yet she lays only a few eggs and guards them.

flow.context: This is the last step of Two Out of Thousands. Here you ask where the other young went, and why prey animals have so many.

activities.title: The Ten-Year Wave: draw two lines and find the delay
activities.context: In this activity you plot the numbers of hares and of lynx over 20 years on one graph. A lynx is a wild cat who hunts hares. The numbers are made up, but they are shaped like real records kept by fur traders in Canada.

materials.item: a sheet of squared or graph paper
a ruler, a pencil and two colour pencils

activities.record: Keep the graph. Under the graph, write how many years pass between two hare peaks. Also write how many years later the lynx peak comes.

example_chart.title: Numbers to plot (made up, in thousands, shaped like the real fur records)

setup.art: A sheet of graph paper with years 1 to 20 along the bottom and numbers 0 to 100 up the side, and a table of numbers beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the axes. Years go along the bottom, thousands of animals up the side.

setup.art: The same graph with a tall wavy line in one colour for hares and a lower wavy line in another colour for lynx, the lynx peaks a little to the right of the hare peaks.
setup.caption: 2. Plot the hares in one colour and the lynx in another. Compare the peaks.

flow.do: 1. Draw a line along the bottom of the paper and mark years 1 to 20. 2. Draw a line up the side and mark 0 to 100 in tens. 3. Before plotting, ask for a guess. When hares become many, what will happen to the lynx, and when?
flow.say: A lynx eats hares. When there are many hares, what will happen to the number of lynx? Will it happen in the same year, or later? Why?
flow.kid: Draw the two axes. Mark years 1 to 20 along the bottom. Mark 0 to 100 up the side. When hares are many, what happens to the lynx? When?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ten-Year Wave. Here you draw the axes of a graph and guess how lynx numbers will follow hare numbers.

flow.do: 1. Plot the 20 hare numbers as dots and join them in one colour. 2. Plot the 20 lynx numbers and join them in a second colour. 3. Mark each peak, the highest point of each wave.
flow.say: Plot the hares first, then the lynx. Then find the top of each wave.
flow.kid: Plot the hare numbers. Join the dots. Plot the lynx numbers in another colour. Mark the top of each wave.
flow.context: This step of the Ten-Year Wave plots hares and lynx for 20 years, as two lines on one graph.

flow.do: 1. Count the years from one hare peak to the next. 2. Count the years from a hare peak to the lynx peak that follows. 3. Ask why the lynx peak comes later, and why the hares crash.
flow.say: How many years is it from one hare peak to the next? How long after the hares do the lynx reach their peak? Why are they late?
flow.kid: Count the years between two hare peaks. Count how late the lynx peak is. Why are the lynx late?

ask.q: Why does the lynx peak come after the hare peak?
good: Lynx need time to raise more kittens after the food increases.
The eaters follow their food late.

ask.q: Why might the hares crash after their peak?
good: Many hares eat down their food plants.
By then there are many lynx hunting them.

flow.parent: The hare peaks are at years 4 and 14, so the wave is 10 years long. The lynx peaks are at years 6 and 16, so the lynx are 2 years late. In the real records the delay is one or two years. Scientists have found that both hunger and predators help to cause the hare crash.

check.q: On a graph of hares and the lynx who eat them, where is the lynx peak?
options: Just after the hare peak
Just before the hare peak
At the lowest point for hares
check.why: More hares means more food, so more lynx kittens live. But raising young takes time, so the lynx reach their peak a year or two after the hares.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Ten-Year Wave. Here you measure the length of the wave and the delay between the hares and the lynx.

activities.title: A New Arrival: add lantana to the web
activities.context: In this activity you add a new being to the wide web from the Two Webs Test. Lantana is a garden shrub from the Americas that now spreads through Indian forests. You work out who gains and who loses.

materials.item: the wide web sheet from the Two Webs Test (or draw it again: 10 forest beings and 18 arrows)
a slip of paper marked LANTANA
coins

activities.record: Write a chain of changes that starts with 'lantana spreads'.

setup.art: The wide web sheet with a paper slip marked LANTANA placed half over the word Grass.
setup.caption: 1. Put the lantana slip half over the grass. Lantana shades out grass.

setup.art: The same sheet with coins showing tails on grass, hare, chital and grasshopper, and a child placing a coin on the leopard.
setup.caption: 2. Follow the change with coins. Heads means more, tails means fewer.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the wide web sheet. 2. Give three facts about lantana. Lantana grows in thick bushes and shades out grass. Deer, hares and cattle avoid eating the leaves. Some birds eat the berries. 3. Ask for a guess. Who in the web will gain, and who will lose?
flow.say: Lantana is new to this forest. Grass cannot grow in lantana's shade. Deer and hares do not eat lantana leaves. Who do you think will gain? Who will lose? Why?
flow.kid: Lantana is a new shrub in the forest. Lantana shades out the grass. Deer and hares do not eat lantana. Who will gain? Who will lose?
flow.context: This is the first step of A New Arrival. Here you learn three facts about lantana and guess who in the forest web will gain or lose.

flow.do: 1. Put the lantana slip half over Grass. Put a coin tails up on Grass, for 'fewer'. 2. Use the two rules to follow the change upwards. Less food means fewer eaters. Fewer eaters means more of their food. 3. Put a coin on every being who changes.
flow.say: The grass is less. Who eats grass? What happens to them? And who eats them?
flow.kid: Put the lantana slip half over Grass. Grass becomes less. Who eats grass? Put a coin on each being who changes.
flow.parent: A good chain: less grass, so fewer grasshoppers, hares and chital. The chital and the hare still have shrubs, and the chital has figs, so they do not vanish. Fewer chital and hares mean less food for the dhole and the leopard. Birds who eat the berries may gain a little.
flow.context: This is the main step of A New Arrival. You place lantana over the grass in the wide web and follow the change up to the predators.

flow.do: 1. Ask why lantana spreads so fast in India. 2. Ask what could hold lantana back. 3. Tell your child what people do: in some forests, teams pull the bushes out by the root, and grass returns.
flow.say: In the Americas, lantana does not take over like this. What might be missing here?
flow.kid: Why does lantana spread so fast here? What is missing? What could hold lantana back?

ask.q: Why does lantana spread so fast in India?
good: The insects and illnesses that feed on lantana in the Americas are not here.
Almost nobody in the web eats the leaves, so nothing pushes back.

check.q: Why can a plant brought from far away spread so fast in a new place?
options: Their usual eaters were left behind
The new soil is always richer
New plants grow faster than old ones
check.why: In their old home, insects, grazers and illnesses hold a plant's numbers down. In a new place those may be missing, so there is little feedback to stop the plant spreading.

flow.context: This is the last step of A New Arrival. Here you ask why lantana spreads so fast in India and what could hold lantana back.

activities.title: If the Forest Is Cut: a map of what follows
activities.context: In this activity you start from one change, a forest being cut down, and map everything that follows from it. Each slip of paper holds one result, and each result leads to more.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper or a clear patch of floor
small slips of paper
a pencil

activities.record: Copy the finished map into your notebook, with an arrow from each cause to its result.

setup.art: A slip of paper in the middle of a floor that reads 'The forest is cut', with three slips around it: 'No leaves or fruit', 'No shade or nests', 'Bare soil'.
setup.caption: 1. Put the first change in the middle. Add what follows at once.

setup.art: The same floor with about twelve slips spreading outward in rings, joined by pencil arrows on a big sheet.
setup.caption: 2. For each slip, ask 'and then what?' Add another ring.

flow.do: 1. Write 'The forest is cut' on a slip and put it in the middle. 2. Ask what is lost at once when the trees go. 3. Write each answer on its own slip and place the slips around the first one.
flow.say: A forest has been cut down. What is gone straight away? Think of food, of homes, and of the ground.
flow.kid: Write 'The forest is cut' on a slip. What is lost at once? Write each answer on a new slip. Put the slips around the first one.
flow.parent: The first answers are these. There are no leaves, fruit or seeds to eat. There is no shade, no nest and no hiding place. The soil is bare, with no roots or fallen leaves. And fewer leaves are left to give out water vapour and take in carbon dioxide.
flow.context: This is the first step of If the Forest Is Cut. Here you write down what is lost at once when a forest is cut.

flow.do: 1. Point to each slip in turn and ask, 'And then what?' 2. Write each new result on a slip and place it further out. 3. Draw an arrow from each cause to its result. 4. Go on until you have at least 12 slips.
flow.say: The herbivores have no leaves to eat. And then what? The soil is bare. What happens when heavy rain falls on it?
flow.kid: Point to each slip. Ask 'and then what?' Write the new result. Place it further out. Make at least 12 slips.
flow.parent: The next answers are these. Herbivores starve or leave. Then carnivores have no prey. Animals come into fields and villages for food. Rain runs off bare soil, so floods are worse and the soil washes away. Less water soaks in, so wells and streams dry sooner. More carbon dioxide stays in the air.
flow.context: This is the main step of If the Forest Is Cut. For each result you ask what follows next, and the map grows outward.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to find the longest chain of arrows on the map. 2. Ask which results reach people. 3. Ask what could be done to stop each chain early.
flow.say: Which chain is the longest? Which of these results would reach a family in a town far away?
flow.kid: Find the longest chain on your map. Which results reach people in towns? What could stop the chain early?

check.q: A forest is cut down. Why do the carnivores there suffer, though they never eat plants?
options: Their prey lose food and shelter
Carnivores eat wood in winter
Carnivores need shade to hunt
check.why: The plants fed the herbivores, and the herbivores fed the carnivores. When the producers go, the loss passes up every chain. This is an indirect effect.

flow.context: This is the last step of If the Forest Is Cut. Here you find the longest chain on your map and see which results reach people.

projects.title: My Place, My Web: map and test a real food web
projects.context: In this four-day project you choose one real place and map who eats whom there. Then you measure your web and test what would happen if one being were lost.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a large sheet of paper for the final web
colour pencils
coins or buttons for the test
a book about animals, a grown-up who knows the place, or the internet with a grown-up

schedule.what: Choose a place. List 10 to 12 living beings there, with at least 2 producers.
Find out what each being eats. Watch, ask, or look it up. Write each link down.
Draw the web. Count the beings and the links. Find the being with the most arrows.
Take one being out and follow the change. Write a short report.

projects.record: Keep the list, the web drawing and a half-page report. The report says which being you removed, who changed, and how sure you are.

setup.art: A child at a window with a notebook, listing beings seen in a neem tree outside: a crow, a squirrel, ants, a garden lizard.
setup.caption: 1. Choose a place and list who lives there.

setup.art: A large sheet of paper with a hand-drawn food web of about twelve beings, arrows in colour, and coins on the names.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the web, count the links, then take one being out.

flow.do: 1. Choose one place. It can be a tree on your street, a pond or a paddy field you know. It can also be a famous place, such as Chilika lake. 2. List 10 to 12 living beings who live there. 3. Make sure the list has at least 2 producers and at least 2 animals who eat other animals.
flow.say: Which place shall we map? Who lives there? Remember the plants, and remember the very small animals.
flow.kid: Choose one place. List 10 to 12 living beings there. Include 2 plants. Include 2 animals who eat other animals.
flow.parent: A ready list for Chilika lake in Odisha, if you cannot watch a place. Seagrass and tiny floating algae are the producers. Tiny floating animals eat the algae. Prawns and mullet fish eat algae and rotting plants. Small fish eat the tiny animals. Crabs eat rotting plants and small animals. Big fish eat small fish and prawns. Irrawaddy dolphins eat fish and prawns. Sea eagles eat fish. Flamingos eat algae and tiny animals. Ducks eat seagrass. People catch fish, prawns and crabs.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Place, My Web. Here you choose a real place and list the living beings there.

flow.do: 1. For each animal on the list, find out what they eat. 2. Watch if you can. Ask someone who knows the place. Look in a book or online with a grown-up. 3. Write each link as 'food → eater'. 4. Put a question mark beside any link you are not sure of.
flow.say: How do we know what she eats? Did we see it, did someone tell us, or did we read it?
flow.kid: Find out what each animal eats. Watch, ask or read. Write each link as food → eater. Mark the ones you are unsure of.
flow.parent: Marking unsure links matters. Real scientists find links by watching, and by studying droppings and stomachs. Many links in published webs are still guesses.
flow.context: This step of My Place, My Web finds out what each being on your list eats. You write down each link.

flow.do: 1. Draw the web on the large sheet, with producers at the bottom. 2. Draw every arrow from the food to the eater. 3. Count the beings and the arrows, and divide arrows by beings. 4. Circle the being with the most arrows going in and out.
flow.say: How many links does our web have for each being? Who has the most arrows? What might that mean?
flow.kid: Draw the web with plants at the bottom. Draw every arrow. Count beings and arrows. Circle the being with the most arrows.
flow.context: This step of My Place, My Web draws the web and measures it by counting the beings and the links.

flow.do: 1. Put a coin on every being. 2. Choose one being to remove, and guess who will change. 3. Use the hunger rule and the two rules to follow the change. 4. Write a half-page report. Say who changed, and how sure you are.
flow.say: Which being shall we take out? Who do you think will change, and why? Let's follow it through the web.
flow.kid: Put a coin on every being. Take one being out. Who goes hungry? Who becomes more? Write a short report.

ask.q: How sure are you of your result? What would make you more sure?
good: Not very sure, because some links are guesses.
Counting the animals for some years, or comparing with a place that lost that being.

flow.parent: The hunger rule: an animal with no food left is lost. The two rules: fewer eaters means more of their food, and less food means fewer eaters. A strong report admits what the paper web cannot show.
flow.context: This is the last step of My Place, My Web. Here you remove one being from your web, follow the change and write a short report.

challenges.title: A Web That Holds: 8 beings, 12 arrows
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the Two Webs Test, the web with more arrows lost fewer beings. Here you have only 12 arrows. You must place them so that your web loses as few beings as possible.
challenges.problem: Design a food web with 2 producers and 6 animals, joined by exactly 12 arrows. When any 2 beings are taken away, as few others as possible should be lost to hunger.
constraints: Every animal must have at least one food, and every arrow goes from a food to an eater.
At least 2 of the animals must eat other animals.
Test with 5 draws of 2 name cards, using the hunger rule: an animal with no food left is lost.
general: Give every animal exactly two foods.
Let both producers feed several herbivores.
Give the top predator two different prey.
creative: Add an omnivore who eats one plant and one animal.
Give three foods to the animal that most others depend on.
Make sure no animal depends only on another animal with one food.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own web. Draw it, test it with 5 draws and write the average number of beings left. Then move one arrow and test again. Did it improve?

setup.art: A sheet of paper with two plants at the bottom and six made-up animals above, joined by twelve pencil arrows.
setup.caption: 1. Draw 2 producers, 6 animals and exactly 12 arrows.

setup.art: The same web with coins on the names, two coins removed and a child checking whether a third animal still has food.
setup.caption: 2. Draw 2 name cards, remove them, and use the hunger rule.

flow.do: 1. Choose 2 producers and 6 animals. They can be real or made up. 2. Draw them with producers at the bottom. 3. Add exactly 12 arrows from foods to eaters. 4. Write the 8 names on 8 cards.
flow.say: You have only 12 arrows. Where will each one do the most good? Why?
flow.kid: Choose 2 plants and 6 animals. Draw them. Add exactly 12 arrows. Write the 8 names on cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Web That Holds. Here you draw your own web of 8 beings joined by exactly 12 arrows.

flow.do: 1. Put a coin on every being. 2. Shake the cards and draw 2. Remove those coins. 3. Use the hunger rule until nobody else is lost. 4. Count who is left and write it down. 5. Do this 5 times and find the average.
flow.say: Two beings are gone. Does anyone have no food left? Check again after each loss.
flow.kid: Put a coin on every being. Draw 2 cards. Remove those coins. Remove any animal with no food left. Count who is left. Do it 5 times.
flow.parent: The best possible score is 6 left. A web where every animal has two different foods scores 5 or 6 in nearly every draw.
flow.context: This step of A Web That Holds tests your design. You remove 2 beings at random, 5 times, and count who is left.

flow.do: 1. Find the animal who was lost most often. 2. Move one arrow to help that animal. 3. Test 5 more times. 4. Compare the two averages.
flow.say: Who was lost most often? Why? Which arrow would you move to help?
flow.kid: Who was lost most often? Move one arrow to help. Test 5 more times. Compare your averages.

check.q: You have a fixed number of arrows. Which design loses the fewest animals to hunger?
options: One animal gets nearly all the arrows
Every animal gets at least two foods
All the animals eat the same plant
check.why: An animal with two foods still eats when one food is lost. If all the animals eat the same plant, losing that plant starves everyone. If one animal has most of the arrows, the others are left with one food each.

flow.context: This is the last step of A Web That Holds. Here you move one arrow to help the animal lost most often, and test again.

challenges.title: An Owl Perch for the Paddy Field
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. Farmers in Tamil Nadu put T-shaped perches in paddy fields. Owls sit on them at night and watch for rats. Here you build a model perch from newspaper.
challenges.problem: Build a T-shaped perch from newspaper. It must stand in a pot of soil with its bar at least 30 cm above the soil. It must hold a potato on the bar for one minute.
constraints: Use only 4 sheets of newspaper, sticky tape and thread.
The perch stands by itself in a pot of soil, or in a dabba filled with rice. Nobody may hold it.
The potato, about 150 grams, sits on the bar for one minute without falling.
materials: a flower pot of soil, or a dabba filled with rice
general: Roll each sheet tightly from one corner into a thin, stiff tube, and tape it.
Tie and tape the bar across the top of the pole to make a T.
Push the pole deep into the soil.
creative: Add two slanting braces under the bar, to make triangles.
Use two poles with the bar across both, like a goalpost.
Make the bar from two tubes side by side, so the potato does not roll off.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own perch. Draw it, build it and test it with the potato for one minute. Then try to make it taller. How tall can it be and still hold the potato?

setup.art: Hands rolling a sheet of newspaper tightly from one corner into a thin tube, with tape nearby.
setup.caption: 1. Roll newspaper into tight tubes and tape them.

setup.art: A T-shaped newspaper perch standing in a flower pot of soil, with a potato balanced on the bar and a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Stand the perch in a pot. Put the potato on the bar for one minute.

flow.do: 1. Talk about why a farmer wants owls in her field. 2. Ask what an owl needs from a perch. 3. Ask your child to sketch a design before building.
flow.say: An owl hunts by sitting still and listening. What does she need from a perch? Sketch your idea first.
flow.kid: Why does a farmer want owls? What does an owl need from a perch? Sketch your design.

ask.q: What does the farmer gain from the owl, and the owl from the farmer?
good: The owl eats rats who would eat the paddy.
The owl gets a high place to watch from, in a field with no trees.

flow.context: This is the first step of An Owl Perch for the Paddy Field. Here you think about what an owl needs and sketch a design.

flow.do: 1. Roll the newspaper into tight tubes and tape them. 2. Join a pole and a bar into a T. 3. Push the pole into the pot of soil. 4. Measure the height of the bar above the soil. 5. Put the potato on the bar and time one minute.
flow.say: Build your first design and test it. If it bends or tips, look closely at where it gave way.
flow.kid: Roll tight paper tubes. Join them into a T. Stand it in the pot. Measure the bar's height. Put the potato on for one minute.
flow.parent: A sheet rolled tightly from the corner makes a much stiffer tube than a loose roll. The usual weak spots are the joint of the T and a pole that leans in loose soil. Let your child find them.
flow.context: This step of An Owl Perch for the Paddy Field builds the perch from newspaper. A potato tests it.

flow.do: 1. Improve the weakest part and test again. 2. Ask what poison put out for the rats would do to an owl on this perch. 3. Ask which lasts longer, a perch or a packet of poison.
flow.say: What was the weakest part? How did you fix it? Now think about the real field. What would rat poison do to the owl?
flow.kid: Fix the weakest part. Test again. What would rat poison do to the owl?

check.q: A farmer puts out rat poison in a field where owls hunt. What can happen to the owls?
options: Nothing, because owls do not eat poison
Owls who eat poisoned rats can die
The owls become stronger
check.why: The poison passes along the food link from the rat to the owl. With fewer owls, the rats that are left can multiply again. A perch keeps the hunters alive.

flow.context: This is the last step of An Owl Perch for the Paddy Field. Here you improve your perch and think about owls, rats and poison.

items.p: In a food web, what does an arrow from grass to hare mean?
opts: The hare hides in the grass
items.why: An arrow points from the food to the eater, the way the food goes. Reading it backwards is a common slip, because we think of the hunter going towards the food.

items.p: True or false: every food chain in a web starts with a producer.
items.why: True. Only producers make food from sunlight, air and water. A strong answer adds that every animal eats plants, or eats animals who ate plants.

items.p: An animal who eats both plants and animals is called an ____.
items.why: 'Omni' means 'all'. Crows, bears and humans are omnivores.

items.p: Sort these animals by what they eat.
items.a: see items
items.why: Chital and elephants eat only plants. Frogs and leopards eat only animals. Crows and bears eat both. Vultures and hyenas eat animals who are already dead.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words are needed to talk about any food web. A strong answer could give an example of each from a paddy field.
pairs: makes food from sunlight, air and water
eats animals who are already dead
breaks dead things down into the soil

items.p: Sea otters eat sea urchins, and urchins eat kelp. Hunters kill most of the otters. What happens to the kelp?
items.why: With few otters, the urchins multiply and eat the kelp down. Choosing 'grows thicker' means following only one step. The change passes down two links.

items.p: In the Two Webs Test, the wide web had more beings left. Explain why, using the word 'food'.
items.a: In the wide web, most animals had more than one food. When one food was taken away, they still had another to eat. In the narrow web each animal had only one food, so they starved when that food went.
items.why: A strong answer says that the number of foods each eater has made the difference. It uses a result from the test.

items.p: Draw a food web with 2 plants and 4 animals. Draw every arrow from the food to the eater.
items.a: A web with two producers at the bottom and four animals above. Each animal has at least one arrow coming in from a food.
items.why: A strong drawing has every arrow pointing from the food to the eater. Every path starts at a plant, and at least one animal has two foods.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

items.p: Three of these are consumers. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: A paddy plant is a producer, who makes their own food. The frog, the owl and the rat must all eat other living beings.

items.p: True or false: a frog is a herbivore, because frogs are small.
items.why: False. A frog eats insects, and insects are animals, so a frog is a carnivore. The group does not depend on size.

items.p: A forest loses all its leopards and dholes. Put what follows in order.
a: The chital eat down the grass and shrubs
The chital run short of food
items.why: With no predators, the herbivores increase until they eat down the plants. Then they starve. Removing the top of a web harms the bottom, and then the middle.
items: The chital run short of food
The chital eat down the grass and shrubs

items.p: A change that reaches a being through a third being in between is called an ____ effect.
items.why: A direct effect passes along one link. An indirect effect passes through someone in between, as from a snake through the rats to the paddy.

items.p: A rat snake is found in a paddy field. Two neighbours disagree about what to do.
items.a: A strong answer uses the web: the snake eats rats, and rats eat paddy, so killing the snake costs grain. It also takes the fear seriously: some snakes are dangerous, so people should learn to tell them apart and wear shoes in the field.
items.why: Both neighbours care about the village. The web shows what killing the snake would cost, and the fear shows what people need to feel safe.

views.says: Kill the snake. Some snakes are dangerous, and children play near this field.
Leave him alone. Rat snakes are harmless, and he eats the rats who eat our paddy.

items.ask: Which neighbour do you agree with? Use the food web of the field. Then say one thing the other neighbour has right.

items.p: Why does a frog lay thousands of eggs, while a tigress has only two to four cubs?
opts: Frogs live much longer than tigers
Most frog eggs and tadpoles are eaten
Tigers have less food than frogs
items.why: Most of a frog's young become food for others, so she needs thousands for a few to be left. A tigress's cubs are seldom eaten, and she guards each one.

items.p: In the Leaky Bottle, the level stayed still while water ran through. How is a deer herd like that?
items.a: Fawns are born and deer die all the time, like water running in and out. If births and deaths match, the number of deer stays about the same, like the water level.
items.why: A strong answer matches the tap to births, the hole to deaths and the level to the number of deer.

items.p: Owls eat rats, and rats eat paddy. All the owls leave a field. Which is the indirect effect?
items.why: More rats is the direct effect, along one link. Less paddy is indirect, because it reaches the paddy through the rats.

items.p: Insect poison sprayed on paddy also kills the spiders. Explain why the plant-sucking insects may then become more, not fewer.
items.a: Spiders eat the plant-sucking insects. The poison kills the spiders as well as some of the insects. The insects who are left breed quickly, and now few spiders are there to eat them.
items.why: A strong answer names the link from the insect to the spider. It says that prey usually multiply faster than their predators.

items.p: True or false: a keystone species is always the most common animal in a place.
items.why: False. A keystone species is often few in number. What marks them is how much the web changes when they are lost.

items.p: A specialist eats one food. An eater of many kinds of food is called a ____.
items.why: A generalist can turn to another food when one is lost. Crows, rats and humans are generalists.

items.p: Specialist or generalist? Sort these eaters.
items.a: see items
items.why: A koala eats eucalyptus leaves, a giant panda eats bamboo and a silkworm eats mulberry leaves. Crows, house rats and humans eat many kinds of food.

items.p: Hares peak in year 4. The lynx who eat them peak in year 6. Why are the lynx late?
items.why: More food lets more lynx kittens live, but kittens take time to be born and grow. So the number of eaters follows the food late.

items.p: Sketch a line graph of ants at a sugar drop. The sugar is removed at 16 minutes. Mark that point.
items.a: A line that rises slowly, then quickly, and levels off. After the mark at 16 minutes the line falls slowly, not straight down.
items.why: A strong sketch shows the slow start and the slow fall after the food is gone. Both show that eaters follow their food late.
items.art: Blank graph axes labelled Minutes and Ants.

items.p: Rats are eating the paddy in a village. Three people suggest what to do.
items.a: A strong answer sees that poison works fast but can kill the owls and snakes. Then the rats return with fewer hunters. Owls and snakes work every night, but they cannot stop a sudden flood of rats alone. It chooses a plan for one season and a plan for ten years, and says why they differ.
items.why: There is a real trade-off between a quick fix and keeping the web's own rat-catchers alive.

views.says: Poison kills hundreds of rats in one night. My crop cannot wait for owls.

views.who: A farmer who puts up owl perches
views.says: Owls and snakes hunt every night for nothing. Poisoned rats kill my owls.
Rats breed faster than owls. Keep the owls alive, and use traps and tight grain stores as well.

items.ask: Which plan would you choose for this one season? Which for the next ten years? Give your reasons.

items.p: The bamboo in Mizoram fruits all at once. Put what follows in order.
a: The rats move into the rice fields
The rats starve and become few
items.why: A flood of food at the bottom raises the eaters. When that food ends, the eaters move along another link, and then crash.
items: The rats move into the rice fields
The rats starve and become few

items.p: A second hole lowered the level in the Leaky Bottle. What change in a forest is like a second hole?
items.a: A new cause of death that stays, such as a new predator, a disease or hunting. The population settles at a new, lower number.
items.why: A strong answer names a lasting change. It says the number settles at a new level and does not return to the old one.

items.p: Match each change that people made to what followed.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of these really happened. In every case the change passed on to beings that nobody had meant to harm.
pairs: Urchins ate down the kelp forests
Starfish were removed from a shore
Stray dogs fed on the dead cattle
Nile perch were put in a lake
Many kinds of small fish died out

items.p: A pond's frogs stay the same in number. One pair leaves 4,000 eggs. About how many become parents?
items.why: Two parents are replaced by about two young. If more lived, the number of frogs would grow every year. Choosing 2,000 means halving the eggs, but nearly all the eggs are eaten.

items.p: Three of these were brought to India by people and then spread widely. Which one was not?
items.why: Neem is native to India. Lantana and water hyacinth came from the Americas, and the giant African snail from Africa.

items.p: Hunters kill most sea otters. Label each being 'more' or 'fewer': kelp → sea urchin → sea otter.
items.why: Each step down the chain flips. Fewer otters means more urchins, and more urchins means less kelp.
items.art: The chain kelp → sea urchin → sea otter drawn large, with a blank box under each being.

items.p: The Two Webs Test followed hunger only. Name one thing in a real forest that the test left out.
items.a: When predators are lost, their prey can multiply and eat down the plants. Animals can also move away, find new foods or die of disease.
items.why: A strong answer names a real effect the paper model cannot show, such as prey multiplying when a predator goes.

items.p: A scientist removes starfish from one stretch of shore and leaves the next untouched. Why is the untouched stretch needed?
items.a: Without that stretch, nobody could tell what caused the change. It might be the missing starfish, or something else, such as the weather that year. The untouched stretch shows what happens when nothing is removed.
items.why: A strong answer says the two stretches differ in only one thing, so that one thing must be the cause.

items.p: Does a food web with more links stay steadier? Two scientists disagree.
items.a: A strong answer says the Two Webs Test supports the forest ecologist, because the wide web lost fewer beings. It then says the test measured only hunger after a loss. It did not measure how much numbers swing, or how a disease or poison spreads along links.
items.why: Both are partly right. The answer depends on what 'steady' means and on how strong the links are.

views.says: Yes. If one food fails, eaters switch to another. Fields of a single crop suffer the worst pest outbreaks.
No. In my equations, more links give a disturbance more paths to spread, and the numbers swing more.

items.ask: Which view does your Two Webs Test support? What did the test not measure? Then say which view you find stronger.

items.p: Which test would best show whether owl perches reduce rats in paddy fields?
opts: Ask one farmer what she thinks
Count the rats in one field once
Compare similar fields with and without perches
Count the owls in a zoo
items.why: Comparing similar fields that differ only in the perches is a fair test. One farmer's opinion or one count cannot separate the perches from the weather or the season.

items.p: Losing the snakes pushes the paddy down by one path and up by another. How could you find the stronger path?
items.a: Compare real fields with snakes and without snakes. Measure the harvest and count the rats and grasshoppers in each, for a few seasons.
items.why: A strong answer says a drawing cannot settle it, and proposes measuring real fields that differ only in the snakes.

items.p: True or false: if a population stays the same size, no animals in that population are dying.
items.why: False. Animals are born and die all the time. The number stays the same when births and deaths match, as the level did in the Leaky Bottle.

items.p: A second equal hole dropped the Leaky Bottle's level from 12 cm to 3 cm. Why not to 6 cm?
opts: Shallow water leaves each hole more slowly
items.why: At 6 cm deep, each jet is only a little slower than at 12 cm. So two holes still let out more than the tap brings in. The level keeps falling until two slow jets together match the tap.

items.p: Mizoram's bamboo fruits all together, once in about 48 years. Give one way this could help the bamboo's seeds.
items.a: There is far more fruit at once than the rats and birds can eat. So many seeds are left to grow. In the long gap between, there is no fruit, so the seed eaters stay few.
items.why: A strong answer says that a flood of food swamps the eaters. It may add that this is an idea that is hard to test.

items.p: When a change causes something that pushes back against that change, this is called ____.
items.why: More deer leads to more deaths, which brings the number of deer back down. That push back is feedback.

items.p: Does each change start at the top of a web or at the bottom? Sort them.
items.a: see items
items.why: A change to an eater starts at the top and passes down. A change to a producer or a food starts at the bottom and passes up.

items.p: Chilli, tomato and lantana all came to India from the Americas. Why is only lantana called invasive?
opts: Lantana spreads unaided and harms other beings
items.why: Invasive does not mean foreign. Chilli and tomato stay where farmers plant them. Lantana spreads through forests without help and shades out the plants already there.

items.p: Put these steps of a removal test in order.
a: Count the living beings in both
Remove one kind from one place only
items.why: First find two matching places and count. Then change one thing in one place. Then count for long enough to see slow effects, and compare.
items: Remove one kind from one place only
Count the living beings in both

items.p: Some people say the world would be better with no rats at all. Use a food web to answer them.
items.a: Owls, snakes, cats and many other animals eat rats, so they would lose food. Rats also eat insects and spread seeds. Rats become a problem where their predators are missing or where there is a flood of food.
items.why: A strong answer shows who depends on rats. It says that 'pest' describes a place and a number, as well as an animal.

items.p: Match each way of studying a food web to what it can show.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each method answers a different question. Ecologists use several together, because each one misses something.
pairs: Remove one kind and keep a second place untouched
what that kind does in the web
Count animals every year for many years
Compare islands with and without a predator
Test a web on paper or on a computer

items.p: Three of these changes add a being to a web. Which one removes a being?
opts: Nile perch are put into a lake
Vultures die from a cattle medicine
Lantana is planted in a garden
items.why: The vultures were lost from the web. The other three are new arrivals. Webs can be changed in both ways.

items.p: The Leaky Bottle is a model of a deer herd. Label what the tap, hole, level and second hole stand for.
a: Water level: the number of deer
Second hole: a new cause of death
items.why: A model is useful only when each part stands for something real. A strong answer can also name one thing the bottle leaves out.

quiz.p: A food web has 10 beings and 18 arrows. What does each arrow show?
opts: One food passing to one eater
quiz.why: Each arrow is one link. It points from a food to an eater of that food.

quiz.p: A jackal hunts hares, eats fruit and feeds on dead animals. Which groups fit a jackal?
quiz.why: Hares and fruit make a jackal an omnivore. Feeding on dead animals makes a jackal a scavenger too. Many animals fit more than one group.

quiz.p: What do decomposers do in a food web?
opts: Return dead matter to the soil
quiz.why: Fungi and bacteria break dead plants and animals down into simple matter. Plants take that matter up again through their roots.

quiz.p: Owls eat rats, and rats eat paddy. More owls come to a field. What is the indirect effect?
quiz.why: Fewer rats is the direct effect. More paddy is the indirect effect, because it reaches the paddy through the rats.

quiz.p: True or false: a leopard can change how much grass grows, without ever eating grass.
quiz.why: True. Leopards eat chital, and chital eat grass. Fewer leopards can mean more chital and less grass. This is an indirect effect.

quiz.p: The grass disappears from two webs. In which web do more animals starve?
opts: Where each animal eats several foods
Where each animal eats one food
quiz.why: An animal with one food starves when that food goes. An animal with several foods can turn to another. That is what the Two Webs Test showed.

quiz.p: A forest has about 500 chital year after year. What must be true?
quiz.why: Chital are born and die all the time. The number stays steady because the two roughly match, as the water level did in the Leaky Bottle.

quiz.p: Why can rats multiply much faster than the owls who eat them?
opts: Rats have many young, several times a year
Rats live much longer than owls
Owls eat only one rat a year
quiz.why: A rat has 6 to 8 young at a time, several times a year. An owl raises a few chicks a year. Prey usually breed faster than their predators.

quiz.p: Hares suddenly have much more food. Hares suddenly get much more food. When will the number of lynx who eat hares rise?
quiz.why: First the hares increase. Then more lynx kittens live and grow. The eaters follow their food late.

quiz.p: Why has lantana spread so widely through India's forests?
quiz.why: Lantana came from the Americas. Deer and cattle here avoid the leaves, so little holds lantana back.

quiz.p: One kind of starfish is removed from a rocky shore for some years. What follows?
opts: More kinds of animals move in
Mussels take over and other kinds are lost
quiz.why: The starfish ate mussels and kept space open on the rock. Without them, mussels crowded the others out. One predator was holding the whole community together.

applications: Farmers in Tamil Nadu and other states put up T-shaped perches in paddy fields. Owls sit on them at night and hunt rats, so less poison is needed.
Forest teams in several Indian tiger reserves pull out lantana by the root, so that grass can return for deer and elephants.
Before bringing back a lost animal or moving one to a new place, wildlife scientists map the food web to see who will be affected.
Rice farmers in many Asian countries now spray less insect poison, so that spiders and other hunters of crop pests stay alive.
Fishery scientists set limits on catches, because taking too many of one kind of fish changes the numbers of the others in the web.
Doctors and health workers use the same thinking for diseases. When India's vultures were lost, stray dogs are thought to have increased, and so did the danger of dog bites.
Park managers count animals every few years. A steady count tells them that births and deaths are roughly matching.

open_questions.q: Can anyone predict what the loss of one kind of living being will do to a real web?
open_questions.why_open: Real webs have thousands of links, strong and weak. Small tests on shores and ponds work, but whole forests and seas still surprise scientists.

open_questions.q: Are food webs with more links steadier?
open_questions.why_open: Mathematics and field studies have given different answers since 1972. The answer seems to depend on what 'steady' means and on how strong the links are.

open_questions.q: Why do the hares and lynx of Canada rise and fall about every ten years?
open_questions.why_open: Predators and food both play a part, and scientists still argue about how much each one matters.

open_questions.q: Why does the bamboo of Mizoram wait about 48 years to flower, and how do the plants all keep time?
open_questions.why_open: Swamping the seed eaters is the leading idea, but a test takes 48 years. Nobody knows how a bamboo counts the years.

open_questions.q: When a web has been badly changed, can it return to what it was?
open_questions.why_open: Some webs recover when the lost animal comes back. Others settle into a new state and stay there, and nobody can yet tell in advance which will happen.

open_questions.q: How many links are there in the food web of one Indian forest?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody has mapped all the insects, fungi and microbes of any forest, so every published web is incomplete.

maths.problem: In six rounds of the Two Webs Test, the narrow web had 5, 6, 3, 5, 5 and 6 left. What is the average?
maths.explain: Add the six rounds: 5 + 6 + 3 + 5 + 5 + 6 = 30. Divide by the number of rounds: 30 ÷ 6 = 5. So on average 5 of the 10 beings were left.
maths.context: This is about the Two Webs Test. There you take the same 3 beings out of two webs, and count who is left. These are made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example results: beings left out of 10

maths.why_maths: One round depends on which cards happen to come out. An average over six rounds shows the pattern behind the luck.

maths.problem: The narrow web has 10 beings and 7 links. The wide web has 10 beings and 18 links. How many links for each being does each web have?
maths.answer: 0.7 in the narrow web and 1.8 in the wide web.
maths.explain: Divide the links by the beings. Narrow web: 7 ÷ 10 = 0.7. Wide web: 18 ÷ 10 = 1.8. The wide web has more than twice as many links for each being.
maths.context: This is about the two paper food webs in the Two Webs Test. Ecologists measure a web by counting the links for each being.
maths.why_maths: Dividing by the number of beings lets you compare webs of different sizes fairly.

maths.problem: In the Leaky Bottle, the level settled at 12 cm with one hole. With two equal holes it settled at 3 cm. If the pattern continues, where would it settle with three holes?
maths.explain: With 1 hole the level is 12. With 2 holes it is 12 ÷ 4 = 3, and 4 is 2 × 2. So with 3 holes, divide by 3 × 3 = 9. 12 ÷ 9 is about 1.3 cm.
maths.context: This is about the Leaky Bottle, where tap water runs into a bottle and out through holes near the base. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Twice the holes did not give half the level. Spotting the real pattern lets you predict a test you have not done.

maths.problem: Suppose the rats in a village double every month while bamboo fruit lasts. There are 100 rats at the start. How many are there after 6 months?
maths.context: This is about the bamboo fruiting in Mizoram, when rats have far more food than usual and multiply fast. Doubling every month is a simple made-up rule.
maths.why_maths: Doubling grows far faster than adding. It shows why trapping 40 rats a week cannot keep up.

maths.problem: A pair of frogs leaves 4,000 eggs, and 2 of the young live to be parents. What fraction live? What percentage is that?
maths.explain: 2 out of 4,000 is the same as 1 out of 2,000. As a percentage: 2 ÷ 4,000 = 0.0005, and 0.0005 × 100 = 0.05%. That is one twentieth of one percent.
maths.context: This is about Two Out of Thousands. There you colour 2 squares for the frogs who live, out of 4,000 eggs.
maths.why_maths: A fraction turns 'hardly any' into a number you can compare with a tigress's 2 cubs in 12.

maths.problem: On the Ten-Year Wave graph, the hares peak in years 4 and 14. The lynx peak in years 6 and 16. The hares peak again in year 24. When should the lynx peak next?
maths.explain: The lynx peak comes 2 years after each hare peak: 4 + 2 = 6 and 14 + 2 = 16. So after a hare peak in year 24, the lynx peak should come in year 24 + 2 = 26.
maths.context: This is about the Ten-Year Wave. There you plot made-up numbers of hares and lynx for 20 years, and find the delay between them.
maths.why_maths: Reading the delay off a graph lets you predict what the eaters will do before it happens.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that removing one animal can change a whole web? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1950s, many ecologists thought that weather and food decided how many kinds of beings a place could hold. Predators, they thought, only trimmed the numbers a little. In the early 1960s a young American scientist, Robert Paine, decided to test this. He chose a rocky shore at Mukkaw Bay, in Washington State. The shore was covered with mussels, barnacles, limpets and seaweeds, and a purple starfish hunted there. Paine chose one stretch of rock and pulled every starfish off with a crowbar. He threw them far out into the sea. He kept doing this for years, and left the next stretch of rock alone to compare. On the untouched rock nothing changed. On the cleared rock, mussels spread and pushed the other animals out. In a few years the number of kinds fell from 15 to 8. The starfish had been eating mussels and keeping space open for everyone else. In 1969 Paine named such an animal a keystone species. Removing things on purpose, with a second place left alone, became a standard way to study food webs.
how_we_found_out.when: The test began in the early 1960s. The results were published in 1966, and the name 'keystone species' in 1969.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That predators only trim the numbers of their prey. People thought predators did not decide which kinds of beings could live in a place. Paine showed that removing one predator changed the whole community.
how_we_found_out.art: A young man in boots on a wet rocky shore at low tide, prying a purple starfish off a rock with a crowbar, with mussels and barnacles around him.

roots.context: We have learned how food webs join living beings, and what happens when one link is lost. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Two Webs Test, the same three beings were taken from both webs. The narrow web then lost more beings to hunger than the wide web did. An eater with one food starved when that food went, and an eater with three foods lived. So the harm done by one loss depends on how many links the rest of the web has.
deep_truth.habit: We call one living being important and another unimportant, or one useful and another a pest. We speak as if that were a fact about that being alone. The test shows that the same loss does little harm in one web and great harm in another. How much a being matters depends on the web around them.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Two Webs Test, losing the grass from the narrow web also starved four animals. Losing the grass from the wide web starved nobody. On Robert Paine's shore, removing one kind of starfish cut the kinds of animals from 15 to 8. On that shore the starfish was the main hunter of mussels, so nobody else could do the same work.

three.who_am_i: You eat many kinds of food, so you are an eater with many links. Each food on your plate joins you to a field, a river or a sea. It joins you to everyone who lives there.
three.what_is_life: No animal feeds alone. Each one lives on those they eat, and feeds those who eat them. Even the young who die early feed someone.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is a web. A change in one place arrives in another place later, often where nobody expected it.

roots.thread: All the food in a web begins as sunlight caught by producers. That one supply of food passes into grass, hare, dhole and leopard. All the food in a web begins as sunlight caught by producers. That one supply of food passes into grass, hare, dhole and leopard. Each of them is built from the same food, in a different body. So the many beings of a forest all live on one shared supply. This is why none of them can be understood alone. To know what one of them does, you have to look at the others they are joined to.

teachings.source: Samyutta Nikaya 12.61, the Buddha's teaching of dependent arising
teachings.teaching: When this is, that is. When this arises, that arises. When this is not, that is not. When this stops, that stops.
teachings.link: This is the rule you used in Take the Snakes Away. When the snakes are gone, something else rises and something else falls. Nothing in a web changes alone.

teachings.source: Tattvartha Sutra 5.21, a Jain text by Umasvati
teachings.teaching: Living beings support one another. In Sanskrit: parasparopagraho jivanam.
teachings.link: A food web shows this support in one form. Every animal is held up by the plants and animals they eat, and holds up those who eat them.

teachings.source: Avatamsaka Sutra, the image of Indra's net
teachings.teaching: A net stretches in every direction, with a jewel at every knot. Each jewel reflects all the other jewels.
teachings.link: In a food web, each being is a knot where links meet. The Two Webs Test showed that what happens at one knot depends on the links around it.

science.text: Removing one kind of living being can change many others who never meet them, through indirect effects.
Whether webs with more links are steadier in every way is still argued about.
Nobody can yet predict exactly what the loss of one being will do to a real web.

other_view.who: Henry Gleason, an American plant scientist, in 1926, and many ecologists since
other_view.view: A forest is not one tightly joined whole. Each kind of plant and animal lives wherever conditions suit them, and they happen to overlap. Most links are weak, and most losses change little. The web is real, but it is loose.

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. The experiments were reasoned through but not tried at home. The Two Webs Test (core) is a paper model, so it always works. I ran every possible draw of 3 cards on a computer. The narrow web keeps about 5 beings on average and the wide web nearly 7, and they tie in about one round in six. The Leaky Bottle (core) needs a tap, a bucket and a grown-up to make two equal holes of about 3 mm. Setting the stream takes patience, and the step says what to do if the bottle overflows or the level stays low. It uses about one bucket of water, which can be kept for mopping or plants. The level with two holes should be near a quarter of the first level, but unequal holes or a drifting tap can make it nearer a third. Ants and the Sugar Drop depends on ants being about. The step says where to look, how long to wait and what to do if none come. Counts differ a lot with the kind of ant. The Ten-Year Wave uses made-up numbers shaped like the real fur records, and says so. The paper perch in An Owl Perch for the Paddy Field needs tightly rolled tubes and a heavy pot, or it tips. Facts checked on 17 Nov 2026: the 15 to 8 kinds on Paine's shore, Estes and Palmisano 1974, the 16 webs in the 2002 study, lantana at more than 40 in 100 of tiger forests, the 1987 frogs' legs ban, the 2006 diclofenac ban, Project Tiger and the 1972 Act, the 48-year Mizoram bamboo cycle with 1959 and 2006 to 2008, the 150 kilograms a day an elephant eats, the Nile perch in the 1950s, and the ginger and turmeric advice of 2007. Softened: Paine's start year (now 'the early 1960s'), the vultures-to-dogs link (now 'thought to'), and how often an elephant calves. The 4,000 frog eggs and the 12 cubs of a tigress are round numbers for the activity. The three videos were found and their titles confirmed on YouTube, but nobody has watched them yet.
